lessons.title: How to use this manual
lessons.html:
This guide is built for the necropsy table. Part I gives the method: history, clinical examination, a fixed step-by-step necropsy routine, correct sampling and a lesion-based differential key. Part II gives one chapter per disease, always in the same order, so you can compare diseases quickly.

Every disease chapter has: an "At a glance" box; cause and epidemiology; clinical (physical) signs; post-mortem lesions organ by organ; pathognomonic or highly suggestive lesions; a differential-diagnosis table; laboratory confirmation (which sample, which test); and treatment, control and prevention.

Photographs are real field and laboratory cases published under open licences. Arrows and letters were added for teaching. Where no open-licence photograph exists, the lesions are described in detail in a table instead; do not use a lesion you have only read about as your sole basis for a diagnosis.

A gross lesion is rarely proof on its own. Few lesions are truly pathognomonic; most diagnoses rest on history + signs + lesions in several birds + laboratory confirmation. The word "pathognomonic" is used in this book only where it is justified; "highly suggestive" is used otherwise.

Notifiable diseases and human safety

Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) and Newcastle disease (ND) are WOAH-listed, notifiable diseases. In Nigeria, report suspicion immediately to the State Director of Veterinary Services and the Federal Department of Veterinary and Pest Control Services; samples for avian influenza go to the national reference laboratory at the National Veterinary Research Institute (NVRI), Vom.

On suspicion of HPAI: stop the necropsy, do not open more birds on the farm, bag and seal carcasses, restrict movement off the farm, and wait for official instructions. Avian influenza viruses (H5N1 and others) can infect people.

Zoonoses you may meet at necropsy: avian influenza, Newcastle disease (conjunctivitis), Chlamydia psittaci, Salmonella, Campylobacter, Mycobacterium avium, Erysipelothrix. Wear protection every time.

lessons.title: The diagnostic approach
lessons.html:
A reliable diagnosis follows the same six steps every time. Skipping the history or the flock observation is the most common reason for a wrong diagnosis.

StepWhat to do
1. HistoryFlock size, age, breed/strain, housing, source of chicks, vaccination record (vaccine, route, date, who gave it), feed source and recent changes, water source, medication, production records (feed/water intake, egg numbers and quality, weights), onset and course, morbidity and mortality by day.
2. Flock observationWatch the flock before handling: distribution, posture, breathing, noises (snicking, rales), droppings, feed and water usage, litter condition, ventilation, smell of ammonia, temperature.
3. Clinical examinationExamine 5–10 live, affected birds: body condition (keel), feathers, skin, comb and wattles (colour, swelling, lesions), eyes and nares, mouth, crop, vent, joints and feet, gait, nervous signs; body temperature if useful (normal about 40.6–41.7 °C).
4. NecropsyOpen at least 5 birds: ideally sick-but-alive birds that you euthanise, plus fresh dead birds. Follow the same routine every time (Section 4) so that nothing is missed.
5. Samples and laboratoryTake samples that answer the question raised by the lesions (Section 5). Keep a record of what was sent, where and when.
6. Tentative diagnosis and actionGive a working diagnosis with a ranked differential list, start control measures that are safe for all likely causes, and review when laboratory results arrive.

Reading the mortality pattern

Pattern in the flockThink first of
Sudden high mortality, few signsHPAI, velogenic ND, acute fowl cholera, heat stress, toxicity (e.g. ionophore overdose, carbon monoxide), water deprivation, electrocution.
Respiratory signs spreading quickly through the houseIB, ND (lentogenic/mesogenic), LPAI (e.g. H9N2), ILT, aMPV; with slower spread: MG, coryza.
Diarrhoea / wet litterCoccidiosis, necrotic enteritis, ND, IBD, salmonellosis, nephropathogenic IB (polyuria), dietary causes, mycotoxins.
Lameness or paralysisMarek's disease, riboflavin deficiency, viral arthritis, MS, staphylococcal/E. coli arthritis, rickets, tibial dyschondroplasia, botulism, AE (young chicks).
Drop in egg production or egg qualityIB, EDS, ND, LPAI, MG, aMPV, heat stress, feed/water problems, mycotoxins.
Peak mortality at 3–6 weeks in broilersIBD, coccidiosis, necrotic enteritis, IBH/HPS (adenovirus), ascites, colibacillosis.

lessons.title: Biosafety, equipment and euthanasia
lessons.html:
Biosafety

  • Do necropsies away from poultry houses (downwind), on a washable table or on a thick plastic sheet you can burn or bury.
  • Wear gloves, a waterproof apron or overall, boots, and a mask (FFP2/N95) and eye protection when respiratory disease or avian influenza is possible.
  • Wet the carcass completely with water containing a little detergent or disinfectant before opening; this stops feathers and dust flying.
  • After work: incinerate or deep-bury carcasses (at least 1 m, with lime), clean and disinfect instruments and the table, wash hands and change clothing before visiting any other flock.

Equipment checklist

  • Strong scissors (one pair blunt-ended, one fine), bone cutters or poultry shears, scalpel, rat-tooth forceps, a small sharp knife.
  • Sterile swabs and tubes with transport medium, sterile containers or bags, 10 % neutral buffered formalin in wide-mouth jars, blood tubes and needles, slides, marker pen, cool box with ice packs.
  • Camera or phone (photograph every lesion with a label or ruler), a record sheet, and disinfectant.

Selecting and euthanasing birds

  • Birds must be killed humanely and without damaging the organs you want to see. Choose the method according to the bird's size and to the samples needed.
  • Cervical dislocation (small birds, done by trained hands): quick stretch-and-twist that separates the skull from the neck. It causes haemorrhage around the neck, so do not use it when the trachea, larynx or brain are the focus.
  • Carbon dioxide in a closed container (rising concentration) or an injectable barbiturate overdose are alternatives that preserve the head and neck.
  • Record the time of death. Fresh carcasses give the best results: autolysis of the intestine starts within an hour in the heat, and after 12–24 hours many lesions (especially intestinal and nervous) cannot be read.

lessons.title: The necropsy, step by step
lessons.html:
Use the same routine on every bird, from the outside in and from the head to the feet. Look first, then touch, then cut. Photograph lesions before you disturb them.

Step 1. External examination

Identify the bird (age, sex, flock). Weigh it. Assess condition by palpating the keel muscles. Look at feathers (lice, mites, feather loss), skin (wounds, pox, cellulitis, cyanosis, haemorrhage), comb and wattles (pale = anaemia or out of lay; cyanotic, swollen, necrotic), eyes (conjunctivitis, swelling, iris colour and pupil shape for Marek's), nostrils and infraorbital sinuses (discharge, swelling), vent (pasting, blood, prolapse), feet and hocks (bumblefoot, swollen joints, scaly-leg mites, haemorrhage on shanks).

Step 2. Head, mouth and upper respiratory tract

Open the beak; examine the mouth, tongue, choanal cleft and pharynx (diphtheritic plaques of wet pox, ulcers, mucus). Cut across the upper beak through the nostrils (just in front of the eyes) and look into the nasal cavity and infraorbital sinus: catarrh, pus, caseous material (coryza, MG, aMPV).

Step 3. Position and skin

Lay the bird on its back. Cut the skin between the thigh and the abdomen on each side and press the legs out and down until the hip joints dislocate so the bird lies flat. Cut the skin across the abdomen and reflect it forward over the breast up to the neck.

Step 4. Subcutis, muscles and neck organs

Check subcutaneous tissue (oedema, cellulitis, haemorrhage, gelatinous fluid, jaundice), breast and thigh muscles (haemorrhages in IBD, pale streaks in myopathy, dehydration). Look at the thymus lobes along the neck (atrophy in immunosuppression) and the crop (content, sour smell, Capillaria, candidiasis "Turkish towel" lining). In young birds note the thyroid and parathyroid glands near the thoracic inlet.

Step 5. Open the body cavity

Cut through the abdominal wall behind the keel, then cut along both sides through the ribs and coracoids with shears, and lift the keel forward and off. Before touching anything, look at the organs in place: smell, fluid (clear, bloody, turbid), yolk or egg material, fibrin, urates, organ positions and colour.

Step 6. Air sacs

Examine the thoracic and abdominal air sacs while they are intact: normally thin and transparent like cling film. Cloudy, thickened, foamy, or with yellow caseous material = airsacculitis (MG, E. coli, IB, aspergillosis plaques).

Step 7. Heart and pericardium

Look at the pericardial sac (fluid, fibrin, urates), then the heart: size and shape (rounded, dilated right ventricle in ascites), petechiae on coronary fat and epicardium (fowl cholera, septicaemias, HPAI), pale streaks or nodules (Marek's tumours, pullorum). Collect heart blood with a sterile syringe for culture if needed.

Step 8. Liver, gall bladder and spleen

Liver: size, colour (normal red-brown; yellow in young chicks with yolk; pale/yellow in fatty liver; bronze-green in fowl typhoid), capsule (fibrin in E. coli, urates in gout), texture (friable), foci (white pinpoint necrosis in fowl cholera, salmonellosis; target-shaped in histomoniasis; tumour nodules), haemorrhages and clots. Spleen (at the junction of proventriculus and gizzard): enlarged, mottled (Marek's, leukosis, salmonellosis, septicaemia), small (IBD, immunosuppression).

Step 9. Remove the digestive tract

Cut the oesophagus near the crop and the rectum in front of the cloaca (leave the bursa in place to examine separately). Lift out the tract with liver and spleen and lay it out straight. Then examine, in order: proventriculus and gizzard (open along the long curvature; wash gently); duodenum and pancreas; jejunum and ileum (with Meckel's diverticulum); both caeca and the caecal tonsils; rectum. Look at the serosa first, then open the gut and examine contents and mucosa. Note lesion position, because in coccidiosis the site identifies the species.

Step 10. Bursa of Fabricius and cloaca

Find the bursa dorsal to the cloaca. Note size (compare with body weight; normal bursa-to-body-weight ratio in broilers is roughly 0.2–0.4 %), colour, oedema, haemorrhage, caseous plugs, nodules. Cut it open. The bursa involutes naturally after sexual maturity, so a small bursa in an adult is normal.

Step 11. Lungs, trachea and larynx

Lungs lie in the ribs: lift them out with blunt forceps. Normal lungs are pink, spongy and float. Look for congestion, oedema, pneumonia (dark red, heavy), yellow nodules (pullorum, aspergillosis). Open the larynx and trachea from the mouth down to the bifurcation with fine scissors: mucus, blood clots (ILT), caseous plugs (IB in chicks, wet pox), haemorrhages (ND, HPAI).

Step 12. Kidneys, ureters and gonads

Kidneys lie in the pelvic bones: note size, colour, pale swollen lobules, urates in tubules and ureters (nephropathogenic IB, gout, dehydration, IBD), tumours. Ovary: follicle appearance (misshapen, haemorrhagic, "cooked" follicles in fowl cholera, pedunculated cysts in pullorum), tumours. Oviduct: size compared with age, contents, cysts (early IB), salpingitis. Testes: size, orchitis.

Step 13. Nerves

Expose the sciatic nerves by removing the muscles on the inside of the thighs (or from above, beside the kidneys, where the sciatic plexus lies). Also look at the brachial plexus near the thoracic inlet and the vagus nerves in the neck. Compare left and right: in Marek's disease the affected nerve is up to 2–3 times thicker, grey-yellow and without its normal cross-striation, and the change is often one-sided.

Step 14. Joints, bones and bone marrow

Open hock, knee and foot-pad joints (turbid fluid, pus, caseous material, blood). Break the tibiotarsus: it should snap cleanly. A bone that bends is soft (rickets, osteoporosis). Split the proximal tibia lengthwise to check the growth plate (widened in rickets, white cartilage plug in tibial dyschondroplasia). Bend the ribs and look for "beading" at the costochondral joints. Look at the marrow colour (pale in anaemia, e.g. chicken infectious anaemia).

Step 15. Brain (when nervous signs are present)

Remove the skin from the head, cut the skull with scissors from the foramen magnum forward on both sides, and lift off the top. Look for haemorrhage, swelling and softening of the cerebellum (vitamin E deficiency, encephalomalacia). Fix half the brain in formalin and keep half chilled for virology.

Step 16. Record and conclude

Write down all findings for each bird, including normal organs. Photograph lesions. Decide on samples before disposing of the carcasses.

lessons.title: Taking samples for the laboratory
lessons.html:
Choose samples that can answer the question raised by the lesions. Label every sample with farm, house, bird number, date, tissue and the test requested, and send a short history with the samples.

PurposeWhat and howUsed for
Bacteriology (culture and sensitivity)Liver, spleen, heart blood, bone marrow, joint fluid, air-sac exudate, yolk sac; take with sterile instruments after searing the organ surface with a hot spatula. Swabs in Amies/Stuart medium. Chill (4 °C), never freeze; deliver within 24–48 h.Colibacillosis, fowl cholera, salmonellosis, staphylococcosis, necrotic enteritis (gut section, anaerobic), coryza (sinus swab).
Virology (isolation, PCR)Tracheal and cloacal swabs, tissues (trachea, lung, kidney, bursa, caecal tonsils, brain, liver) in viral transport medium or dry sterile tubes; chill and deliver within 48 h or freeze at −70 °C (not −20 °C). FTA cards preserve RNA/DNA for PCR without a cold chain.ND, AI, IB, ILT, IBD, adenovirus, reovirus, aMPV, Marek's (feather tips, spleen).
SerologyClotted blood from 10–20 birds of the same age (0.5–1 ml serum each). Paired samples 2–3 weeks apart show a rising titre. Separate serum, keep chilled or frozen.ND and AI (HI test), IB, IBD, MG/MS, EDS (HI), aMPV, reovirus, AE (ELISA); pullorum/typhoid (rapid plate test).
HistopathologySlices no more than 5 mm thick, including the edge of the lesion and normal tissue, in 10 % neutral buffered formalin at a ratio of at least 1 part tissue to 10 parts formalin. Do not freeze.Marek's vs lymphoid leukosis, ILT (inclusions), IBH (inclusions), fowl pox (Bollinger bodies), AE, encephalomalacia, aspergillosis, tumours.
ParasitologyFresh faeces (pooled, from the litter and from birds) for flotation and oocyst counts; mucosal scrapings from lesion sites examined immediately under a cover slip; worms in 70 % alcohol; ectoparasites in alcohol.Coccidiosis, worms, histomoniasis, mites and lice.
Toxicology and feedAt least 500 g of feed from the feeder and from the bin/bag, liver and kidney (frozen), water sample. Keep feed dry and labelled with batch number.Mycotoxins (aflatoxin, ochratoxin), salt, ionophores, excessive calcium, pesticides.

Golden rules of sampling

Sample several birds (at least 5) that are typical of the problem; freshly dead or euthanised, untreated birds are best.

Use sterile instruments for each organ intended for culture; take culture samples before the gut is opened.

Formalin: 1 volume of tissue to 10 volumes of formalin; slices no thicker than 5 mm. Never freeze formalin samples.

Keep bacteriology and virology samples cold (4 °C) and deliver within 24–48 hours.

lessons.title: Lesion terms
lessons.html:
TermMeaning
PetechiaePinpoint haemorrhages (under 1–2 mm).
EcchymosesLarger blotchy haemorrhages (a few mm to 2 cm).
CatarrhalInflammation with excess clear or cloudy mucus.
FibrinousYellow-white, sheet-like or stringy exudate that peels off a surface (e.g. fibrinous pericarditis).
CaseousDry, cheese-like, yellow exudate; typical of birds because heterophils do not form liquid pus.
DiphtheriticA membrane of necrotic tissue and fibrin attached to a mucosa; leaves a raw area when removed.
Necrotic fociSmall grey-white or yellow areas of dead tissue.
OedemaTissue swollen with clear or gelatinous fluid.
HydropericardiumExcess clear fluid in the pericardial sac.
AscitesFluid in the abdominal (peritoneal) cavity.
UratesChalky white uric acid deposits (in kidneys, ureters, on serosae in visceral gout).
PathognomonicA sign or lesion that is found only in one disease and therefore proves it.

lessons.title: Newcastle disease (ND)
lessons.html:
NOTIFIABLE DISEASE

Report suspicion immediately to the veterinary authorities before further necropsies. Handle all material as potentially zoonotic.

Cause: Avian orthoavulavirus 1 (avian paramyxovirus type 1, APMV-1). Pathotypes: velogenic viscerotropic (vvND), velogenic neurotropic, mesogenic, lentogenic (vaccine-like).

At a glance

Key post-mortem picture: Haemorrhages at the tips of the proventricular glands; haemorrhagic-necrotic lymphoid patches and caecal tonsils; nervous signs; green diarrhoea.

Pathognomonic / highly suggestive: None strictly pathognomonic. The combination of proventricular gland-tip haemorrhages + necrotic ulcers over intestinal lymphoid aggregates + caecal tonsil haemorrhage is highly suggestive of vvND, but HPAI can look identical.

Confirm with: RT-PCR (matrix/fusion gene) with sequencing of the F-protein cleavage site; virus isolation in 9–11-day SPF embryonated eggs + HI; ICPI for pathogenicity.

Cause and epidemiology

  • All ages of chickens; endemic in Nigeria and much of Africa and Asia, with outbreaks in poorly or wrongly vaccinated flocks and in village chickens, often in the dry season.
  • Spread by direct contact, aerosols, faeces, contaminated people, crates, egg trays, vehicles and live-bird markets. Incubation 2–15 days (usually 5–6).
  • Morbidity and mortality with vvND can reach 100 % in unvaccinated birds; in vaccinated layers the main sign may be a drop in egg production with poor shell quality.

Clinical (physical) signs

  • Depression, ruffled feathers, off feed, rapid rise in mortality.
  • Respiratory: gasping, coughing, rales, nasal discharge.
  • Digestive: watery green (biliverdin-stained) diarrhoea.
  • Nervous (usually a few days later): twisted neck (torticollis), star-gazing, circling, tremors, paralysis of legs or wings.
  • Oedema of the head and wattles, conjunctivitis, cyanosis in some birds.
  • Layers: sudden fall in egg production, soft-shelled, misshapen and pale eggs, watery albumen.

Post-mortem lesions, step by step

Examine in this order; record positive and negative findings for every bird.

Organ / siteWhat you see
ProventriculusPetechiae and haemorrhages on the tips of the glands (papillae), often at the junction with the gizzard and oesophagus.
GizzardHaemorrhages under the koilin lining and at the proventriculus junction.
IntestineHaemorrhagic, then necrotic and ulcerated oval areas over the lymphoid aggregates (Peyer's patches) visible from the serosa; caecal tonsils swollen, haemorrhagic, necrotic. Duodenal enteritis.
Respiratory tractHaemorrhages and congestion of the trachea; mucus; cloudy air sacs.
Reproductive tractHaemorrhagic, flaccid or degenerating ovarian follicles; yolk in the abdomen (egg peritonitis).
OtherOedema of neck tissues; haemorrhage in the thymus; spleen may be enlarged with necrotic foci. Neurotropic strains may leave no gross lesions.

Pathognomonic and highly suggestive lesions

  • Haemorrhages on the tips of the proventricular glands (highly suggestive of vvND or HPAI).
  • Button-like necrotic ulcers over intestinal lymphoid tissue and necrotic caecal tonsils (highly suggestive of vvND).

Differential diagnosis

DiseaseHow to tell it apart
Highly pathogenic avian influenzaSimilar lesions; more cyanosis and oedema of head, haemorrhages on shanks, pancreatic necrosis. Only the laboratory can separate them.
Acute fowl choleraOlder birds; heart petechiae, liver necrotic foci; bipolar bacteria in liver smears; responds to antibiotics.
Infectious bronchitisRespiratory and egg signs but no proventricular or intestinal haemorrhage and no nervous signs.
Infectious laryngotracheitisBloody tracheitis with clots, no gut lesions.
Infectious bursal diseaseYoung birds; bursal lesions, muscle haemorrhages; haemorrhage at proventriculus–gizzard junction.
Avian encephalomyelitis, vitamin E deficiency, Marek's diseaseCauses of nervous signs; different age and lesions (see those chapters).
Mycoplasmosis, coryzaSlower, milder respiratory disease with sinusitis/airsacculitis, low mortality.

Laboratory confirmation

SampleTestNotes
Tracheal and cloacal swabs, FTA cards; trachea, lung, spleen, caecal tonsil, brainRT-PCR (M gene screen; F gene for virulence); virus isolation in SPF eggsChill, deliver within 48 h. Handle as a notifiable disease.
Serum (10–20 birds, paired)HI test; ELISAInterpret against vaccination history: a high, uneven titre or a rising titre supports field infection.
IsolateICPI (intracerebral pathogenicity index) or F-cleavage site sequenceICPI ≥ 0.7 or multiple basic amino acids at the cleavage site = virulent ND (notifiable).
Fixed tissuesHistopathology, immunohistochemistrySupportive only.

Treatment, control and prevention

  • No treatment. Supportive care (vitamins, electrolytes) and antibiotics only against secondary bacteria.
  • Report to veterinary authorities. Movement restrictions; stamping out in outbreak zones where required.
  • Vaccination: live lentogenic vaccines (e.g. Hitchner B1, LaSota, or thermostable I-2 for village poultry) by eye drop, drinking water or spray, followed by inactivated oil-emulsion vaccines in layers and breeders. Monitor titres by HI.
  • Strict biosecurity: no contact with village birds or live-bird markets, all-in/all-out, clean crates and egg trays.

lessons.title: Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI)
lessons.html:
NOTIFIABLE DISEASE

Report suspicion immediately to the veterinary authorities before further necropsies. Handle all material as potentially zoonotic.

Cause: Influenza A virus (Orthomyxoviridae), subtypes H5 and H7 with a multibasic HA cleavage site (e.g. H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b).

At a glance

Key post-mortem picture: Sudden death with swollen, cyanotic head, comb and wattles; haemorrhages on shanks; widespread haemorrhages and necrosis in internal organs.

Pathognomonic / highly suggestive: Not pathognomonic; lesions overlap with vvND and acute fowl cholera. Treat any such picture as suspect HPAI until proven otherwise.

Confirm with: RT-PCR (matrix gene, then H5/H7 subtyping) at the national reference laboratory; virus isolation; IVPI or HA cleavage site sequencing.

Cause and epidemiology

  • All poultry; wild waterfowl are the reservoir. Nigeria has had repeated H5N1 outbreaks since 2006, mainly in commercial layers and live-bird markets.
  • Spread by wild birds, live-bird markets, people, vehicles, trays and crates. Incubation from a few hours to 7 days (up to 14 days used for regulation).
  • Mortality may approach 100 % within 48–72 hours; in some birds death occurs before any lesion develops.

Clinical (physical) signs

  • Sudden high mortality, often the first sign.
  • Marked depression, huddling, no feed or water intake, sudden stop in egg laying.
  • Swelling (oedema) of the head, face, comb and wattles; cyanosis (purple colour) and necrosis of comb and wattles.
  • Red to purple haemorrhages on the unfeathered skin of shanks and feet.
  • Respiratory distress, nasal discharge, diarrhoea, nervous signs (tremors, incoordination) in some birds.

Post-mortem lesions, step by step

Examine in this order; record positive and negative findings for every bird.

Organ / siteWhat you see
Head and skinSubcutaneous gelatinous oedema of head and neck; cyanotic, haemorrhagic comb and wattles; haemorrhages on shanks.
Respiratory tractHaemorrhagic trachea with mucus; congested, oedematous lungs.
Proventriculus and gutPetechiae on the proventricular gland tips and at the proventriculus–gizzard junction; haemorrhages in intestinal mucosa and caecal tonsils.
Heart and fatPetechiae on the epicardium, coronary fat and abdominal fat.
PancreasPale yellow or haemorrhagic foci of necrosis.
Ovary and oviductHaemorrhagic follicles, yolk peritonitis.
Peracute casesFew or no lesions.

Pathognomonic and highly suggestive lesions

  • No single pathognomonic lesion. Suspect HPAI whenever sudden high mortality is combined with head oedema, cyanosis and shank haemorrhages.

Differential diagnosis

DiseaseHow to tell it apart
Velogenic Newcastle diseaseVery similar; nervous signs more common, intestinal lymphoid necrosis more marked. Laboratory needed.
Acute fowl choleraBipolar organisms in liver impression smears, pinpoint liver necrosis, responds to antibiotics.
Infectious laryngotracheitisClots in trachea; no systemic haemorrhages or head oedema.
Swollen head syndrome (aMPV + E. coli)Swollen head with caseous subcutaneous exudate, low mortality.
Heat stroke, poisoningHistory (temperature, feed change); no infectious spread pattern.

Laboratory confirmation

SampleTestNotes
Oropharyngeal/tracheal and cloacal swabs from dead and sick birds; tissues (brain, lung, trachea, spleen)Real-time RT-PCR (M gene) then H5/H7 subtype PCR; sequencingCollect under full PPE, pack in triple packaging, send to NVRI Vom through the state veterinary services.
SerumHI (H5/H7 antigens), ELISA/AGIDOnly useful in survivors or surveillance; dead flocks rarely have time to seroconvert.
IsolateIVPI or HA cleavage-site sequenceDefines HPAI legally.

Treatment, control and prevention

  • Report immediately; do not treat. Culling of infected and contact flocks, safe disposal, cleaning and disinfection, movement control and zoning by the authorities.
  • Human safety: PPE, avoid handling sick birds, report flu-like illness in workers.
  • Prevention: keep wild birds and ducks away, no visits to live-bird markets, all-in/all-out, footbaths, clean crates and trays. Vaccination only as directed by the national authority.

lessons.title: Low pathogenic avian influenza, H9N2
lessons.html:
Cause: Influenza A virus H9N2 (low pathogenicity, not H5/H7). Endemic in poultry in North and West Africa, the Middle East and Asia, including Nigeria.

At a glance

Key post-mortem picture: Tracheitis with fibrinous/caseous plugs at the tracheal bifurcation; pneumonia; egg drop and egg peritonitis in layers; losses made much worse by secondary E. coli, MG or IB.

Pathognomonic / highly suggestive: None. Diagnosis requires the laboratory.

Confirm with: RT-PCR (M gene, then H9 subtype) on tracheal/oropharyngeal swabs; HI with H9 antigen.

Cause and epidemiology

  • Chickens of all ages; broilers from about 3 weeks of age, layers in production.
  • Mortality alone is usually low (under 5 %) but can reach 20–60 % with secondary bacteria, poor ventilation and co-infection with IB.
  • H9N2 has zoonotic potential and donates internal genes to other influenza viruses; report positive results to the veterinary authorities.

Clinical (physical) signs

  • Respiratory: sneezing, coughing, rales, swollen face, nasal discharge, conjunctivitis.
  • Depression, reduced feed intake.
  • Layers: egg drop (from 5 % to more than 50 %), thin-shelled and pale eggs.

Post-mortem lesions, step by step

Examine in this order; record positive and negative findings for every bird.

Organ / siteWhat you see
TracheaCongested, inflamed mucosa with catarrhal to fibrinous exudate; yellow caseous plug at the bifurcation that can suffocate the bird.
LungsCongestion, oedema, pneumonia; fibrin at the entrance of the bronchi.
HeartEnlarged, especially the right side, secondary to lung oedema.
Air sacsCloudy; fibrinous airsacculitis with secondary E. coli.
Reproductive tract (layers)Oedematous oviduct with catarrhal or fibrinous exudate; ruptured follicles; yolk peritonitis; eggs laid into the abdomen.
Kidneys and gutSwollen kidneys; mild duodenitis.

Pathognomonic and highly suggestive lesions

  • None. Fibrinous tracheal plugs and yolk peritonitis in an affected layer flock are suggestive but also occur in IB, ILT and E. coli infections.

Differential diagnosis

DiseaseHow to tell it apart
Infectious bronchitisSimilar respiratory and egg signs; nephritis more common; separate by PCR.
Newcastle disease (lentogenic/mesogenic)Similar; separate by PCR/HI.
Infectious laryngotracheitisHaemorrhagic tracheitis with blood clots; intranuclear inclusions.
Mycoplasmosis + E. coli (CRD)Slower course, airsacculitis; MG serology/PCR.
aMPV (swollen head)Head swelling, fewer tracheal plugs; serology/PCR.

Laboratory confirmation

SampleTestNotes
Oropharyngeal and tracheal swabs (early), lungs, tracheaReal-time RT-PCR (M gene, H9 gene); virus isolationSample birds in the first days of signs.
Serum (paired)HI with H9 antigenRising titres confirm infection; vaccinated flocks need interpretation.
Air sac, liver, heart bloodBacterial cultureTo guide treatment of secondary E. coli.

Treatment, control and prevention

  • No specific treatment; treat secondary bacteria according to culture and sensitivity; improve ventilation and reduce dust and ammonia; vitamins and electrolytes.
  • Inactivated H9N2 vaccines are used in some countries under official approval.
  • Biosecurity as for HPAI; control of MG, IB and E. coli reduces losses.

lessons.title: Infectious bursal disease (IBD, Gumboro disease)
lessons.html:
Cause: Infectious bursal disease virus (Birnaviridae, Avibirnavirus), serotype 1; classical, variant and very virulent (vvIBDV) strains.

At a glance

Key post-mortem picture: Young birds (3–6 weeks): bursa of Fabricius enlarged, oedematous, yellow or haemorrhagic, later atrophied; haemorrhages in thigh and breast muscles; haemorrhage at the proventriculus–gizzard junction; swollen kidneys with urates.

Pathognomonic / highly suggestive: Acute bursal enlargement with yellow gelatinous peribursal oedema, followed within 7–10 days by atrophy, is highly characteristic of IBD (near-pathognomonic in the right age group).

Confirm with: RT-PCR on bursa (with sequencing to type vvIBDV/variant); histopathology of bursa (lymphoid necrosis); AGID on bursal homogenate; ELISA serology.

Cause and epidemiology

  • Chickens 3–6 weeks old show acute disease; infection before 3 weeks causes silent, severe immunosuppression.
  • Very resistant virus; persists in houses for months. Spread by faeces, litter, people, equipment.
  • Mortality: classical strains 1–10 %, vvIBDV 20–60 % in layers. Sharp peak and fall in deaths within about 7 days is typical.
  • Immunosuppression leads to vaccine failures (ND, IB, MD), gangrenous dermatitis, IBH and other secondary diseases.

Clinical (physical) signs

  • Sudden onset: depression, ruffled feathers, trembling, birds sitting with heads down.
  • Whitish watery diarrhoea with urates; soiled vent; birds peck at their own vent.
  • Dehydration; anorexia; prostration and death within 3–4 days of illness.

Post-mortem lesions, step by step

Examine in this order; record positive and negative findings for every bird.

Organ / siteWhat you see
Bursa of Fabricius (days 2–4)Enlarged up to 2 times normal, turgid, cream-yellow, with yellow gelatinous oedema on the surface and longitudinal striations; may be haemorrhagic ("blood-red bursa") in vvIBDV.
Bursa (days 5–10)Returns to normal size, then atrophies to one-third of normal and turns grey; caseous plugs in the lumen.
MusclesPetechiae and ecchymoses in thigh and breast muscles.
Proventriculus–gizzardHaemorrhages at the junction.
KidneysSwollen, pale, with urates in tubules and ureters (from dehydration).
OtherDehydrated carcass; spleen may be enlarged with grey foci; thymus may be atrophied.

Pathognomonic and highly suggestive lesions

  • Enlarged oedematous bursa with yellow gelatinous transudate in 3–6-week-old chicks, with haemorrhagic leg and breast muscles (highly characteristic).
  • Bursal atrophy in birds under 12 weeks is always significant; compare the bursa with the spleen and with body weight.

Differential diagnosis

DiseaseHow to tell it apart
Newcastle diseaseProventricular gland-tip haemorrhages, lymphoid ulcers in intestine; no bursal oedema.
Nephropathogenic IBSwollen kidneys with urates, respiratory signs; bursa normal.
Chicken infectious anaemia (CAV)Pale bone marrow, thymus atrophy, anaemia (PCV < 27 %), 2–4 weeks.
Mycotoxicosis, sulfonamide toxicityMuscle haemorrhages; history of feed/drugs; no bursal oedema.
CoccidiosisBloody droppings; intestinal lesions.
Marek's diseaseBursa atrophy but with nerve/visceral tumours in older birds.

Laboratory confirmation

SampleTestNotes
Bursa (fresh, chilled or on FTA card)RT-PCR (VP2 gene) with sequencing; antigen-capture ELISA; AGIDSequencing separates vvIBDV, variant and vaccine strains.
Bursa in formalinHistopathology: lymphoid necrosis, oedema, then follicle depletion and fibrosisAlso useful to check vaccine "take".
SerumELISAUsed to time vaccination (maternal antibody; Deventer formula) and to monitor flocks.

Treatment, control and prevention

  • No specific treatment; give electrolytes and water with vitamins, keep feed and water close, reduce stress, and treat secondary infections.
  • Vaccinate breeders so that chicks get high maternal antibody; vaccinate chicks with live intermediate or intermediate-plus vaccines at the right age (based on maternal antibody testing), or use in-ovo/day-old immune-complex or HVT-vectored IBD vaccines.
  • Thorough cleaning and disinfection between flocks; the virus is very resistant, so use aldehyde or iodine-based disinfectants and allow a rest period.

Photographs

lessons.title: Marek's disease (MD)
lessons.html:
Cause: Gallid alphaherpesvirus 2 (Marek's disease virus serotype 1). Spread in feather-follicle dander; very long survival in dust.

At a glance

Key post-mortem picture: Enlarged peripheral nerves (sciatic, brachial, vagus), usually one-sided; lymphoid tumours in liver, spleen, gonads, heart, kidney, skin, muscle, eye; grey iris; paralysis with "split legs".

Pathognomonic / highly suggestive: Unilateral enlargement of peripheral nerves with loss of cross-striation in a bird of the right age is regarded as practically pathognomonic for MD (exclude riboflavin deficiency in young chicks).

Confirm with: Histopathology (pleomorphic lymphoid infiltrate in nerves and tumours); quantitative PCR for MDV-1 (meq gene) in tumours or feather tips; distinguishing from lymphoid leukosis.

Cause and epidemiology

  • Chickens 6–30 weeks old mostly (can be earlier or later). Infection is by inhalation of feather dander in the first days of life, before vaccine immunity develops.
  • Losses from a few percent to over 30 % in unvaccinated or poorly vaccinated flocks; vaccine failures follow poor vaccine handling (liquid nitrogen, mixing, time), early challenge, or immunosuppression (IBD, CAV).

Clinical (physical) signs

  • Progressive asymmetric paralysis: the classic "split legs" posture (one leg forward, one back); drooping wing; twisted neck in some.
  • Weight loss, pale comb, diarrhoea; death from starvation or trampling.
  • Eye: grey, "fish-eye" iris; irregular, small pupil; blindness.
  • Skin: enlarged, nodular feather follicles (skin leukosis) seen at slaughter.
  • Acute form: sudden deaths with large tumours in many organs.

Post-mortem lesions, step by step

Examine in this order; record positive and negative findings for every bird.

Organ / siteWhat you see
Peripheral nervesSciatic plexus and nerve, brachial plexus, vagus: 2–3 times normal thickness, grey or yellow, oedematous, with loss of the normal cross-striations; often one side only.
VisceraDiffuse or nodular white-grey tumours in liver, spleen, gonads (especially ovary: cauliflower-like), heart, lungs, kidneys, proventriculus, muscles.
SkinEnlarged feather follicles with white nodules.
BursaUsually atrophied, sometimes diffusely thickened; nodular bursal tumours point instead to lymphoid leukosis.
EyeGrey iris, irregular pupil.

Pathognomonic and highly suggestive lesions

  • Thickened, grey-yellow peripheral nerves without cross-striations, particularly when one-sided.
  • Grey iris with irregular pupil (ocular MD).

Differential diagnosis

DiseaseHow to tell it apart
Lymphoid leukosisOver 16 weeks old; no nerve lesions; nodular tumours of the bursa; tumours of uniform lymphoblasts (B cells) on histology.
ReticuloendotheliosisUncommon; nerve and visceral lesions possible; PCR.
Riboflavin (vitamin B2) deficiencyYoung chicks (under 3 weeks), curled toes, symmetrical nerve swelling, responds to riboflavin.
Other causes of paralysisViral arthritis, MS, bacterial arthritis, rickets, botulism, spinal abscess; check joints and bones.
Avian TB, coligranulomaCaseous granulomas in liver/intestine rather than soft lymphoid tumours; acid-fast bacilli or E. coli.

Laboratory confirmation

SampleTestNotes
Nerves, tumours in formalinHistopathology: pleomorphic lymphocytes, lymphoblasts, plasma cells ("mixed" population), perivascular infiltration in nervesMain confirmatory test.
Tumour, spleen, feather tips (chilled)qPCR MDV-1 (meq); differentiation from vaccine (CVI988) by specific PCRPresence of virus alone does not prove disease; use with lesions.
TissuesImmunohistochemistry (CD4 T-cells in MD vs IgM B-cells in LL)Separates MD from LL.

Treatment, control and prevention

  • No treatment; cull affected birds.
  • Vaccinate at hatch or in ovo (HVT, bivalent HVT+SB-1, or CVI988/Rispens), with correct thawing, mixing and dosing; give vaccine immunity time to develop (isolate chicks, clean brooders).
  • Brood young chicks away from older birds; all-in/all-out; control IBD and CAV; select resistant genetics.

lessons.title: Avian leukosis (lymphoid leukosis, LL)
lessons.html:
Cause: Avian leukosis virus (Retroviridae, Alpharetrovirus), mainly subgroups A and J. Transmitted vertically through the egg and horizontally.

At a glance

Key post-mortem picture: Birds over 16 weeks (usually in lay): large liver ("big liver disease"), spleen and kidneys with smooth grey-white tumours; nodular tumours in the bursa; no nerve lesions.

Pathognomonic / highly suggestive: Nodular tumours in the bursa of Fabricius are highly characteristic of LL (MD does not form nodular bursal tumours).

Confirm with: Histopathology (uniform lymphoblasts, IgM+ B cells, arising from the bursa); ELISA for p27 antigen in albumen or cloacal swabs; PCR for ALV subgroups.

Cause and epidemiology

  • Adult birds from 16 weeks, peak at sexual maturity; low but steady mortality (1–2 % a month) with loss of egg production.
  • Subgroup J (myelocytomatosis) mainly in meat breeders: chalky yellow-white tumours on bones (sternum, ribs, skull).

Clinical (physical) signs

  • Non-specific: emaciation, pale shrivelled comb, distended abdomen, diarrhoea, drop in lay. No paralysis.

Post-mortem lesions, step by step

Examine in this order; record positive and negative findings for every bird.

Organ / siteWhat you see
LiverGreatly enlarged, diffuse grey-white infiltration or multiple nodules; may be friable and ruptured.
Spleen and kidneysEnlarged with tumours.
BursaNodular tumours (important for diagnosis).
OtherTumours in ovary, heart, lungs, mesentery; subgroup J: tumours on the inner surface of the sternum and ribs.
NervesNormal.

Pathognomonic and highly suggestive lesions

  • Nodular bursal tumours in an adult bird with visceral tumours and normal nerves.

Differential diagnosis

DiseaseHow to tell it apart
Marek's diseaseYounger birds; nerve lesions; ocular and skin forms; mixed-cell tumours (T cells); bursa atrophied.
ReticuloendotheliosisLess common; laboratory differentiation.
Avian tuberculosisCaseous tubercles, acid-fast bacilli.
Ovarian adenocarcinomaOld hens; firm white carcinomatosis on serosae with ascites (see reproductive chapter).
Fatty liver haemorrhagic syndromeYellow friable liver with blood clots; no tumours.

Laboratory confirmation

SampleTestNotes
Tumours in formalinHistopathology and IHCUniform lymphoblasts (LL) vs pleomorphic cells (MD).
Albumen, cloacal swabs, meconiumELISA p27 group-specific antigenUsed in eradication programmes.
Tissue, bloodPCR (subgroup A, J)

Treatment, control and prevention

  • No treatment or vaccine. Control is by eradication in primary breeding stock (testing and removal of shedding hens).
  • Buy stock from leukosis-free breeders; all-in/all-out; hygiene in hatchery.
