lessons.title: Infectious bronchitis (IB)
lessons.html:
Cause: Avian coronavirus (infectious bronchitis virus, IBV), Gammacoronavirus. Many serotypes and genotypes (e.g. Massachusetts, 793B/4-91, QX, Variant 2 in Africa and the Middle East).

At a glance

Key post-mortem picture: Rapidly spreading respiratory disease; in young chicks caseous plugs at the tracheal bifurcation; nephropathogenic strains cause pale swollen kidneys with urates; in layers a drop in production with soft, misshapen and rough eggs and watery albumen; early infection causes cystic oviducts ("false layers").

Pathognomonic / highly suggestive: None. Watery albumen and misshapen, wrinkled eggs in a whole flock are strongly suggestive.

Confirm with: RT-PCR (UTR/N gene) with S1 gene sequencing for genotype; virus isolation in SPF eggs (dwarfing and curling of embryos); serology (ELISA, HI) with paired sera.

Cause and epidemiology

  • All ages; very contagious by aerosol; spreads through a house within 1–2 days. Incubation 18–36 hours.
  • Mortality low in adults, higher in chicks and with nephropathogenic strains (up to 25–30 %) or secondary E. coli.
  • Vaccines protect poorly against different serotypes, so new variants cause outbreaks in vaccinated flocks.

Clinical (physical) signs

  • Chicks: gasping, coughing, tracheal rales, nasal discharge, wet eyes, huddling near heat.
  • Nephropathogenic strains: depression, increased water intake, wet litter with urates.
  • Layers: drop in egg production (up to 50 %) lasting weeks; thin, soft, rough, wrinkled, misshapen or depigmented shells; thin watery albumen.
  • Pullets infected in the first 2 weeks may never lay normally ("false layers" with cystic oviducts).

Post-mortem lesions, step by step

Examine in this order; record positive and negative findings for every bird.

Organ / siteWhat you see
Trachea, nasal passages, sinusesSerous, catarrhal or caseous exudate; caseous plug at the tracheal bifurcation in chicks.
Air sacsCloudy, foamy; yellow caseous exudate with secondary E. coli.
Kidneys (nephropathogenic)Swollen, pale, mottled; tubules and ureters distended with urates; visceral gout in severe cases.
OviductIn layers: shorter, oedematous oviduct; yolk in abdomen. In false layers: cystic, fluid-filled left oviduct.
Proventriculus (QX-like/proventriculitis strains)Enlarged proventriculus in some genotypes.

Pathognomonic and highly suggestive lesions

  • None. Flock pattern of egg-quality changes plus rapid respiratory spread is typical but not specific.

Differential diagnosis

DiseaseHow to tell it apart
Newcastle disease, LPAI H9N2Similar respiratory signs and egg drop; separate by PCR/serology.
ILTHaemorrhagic tracheitis, higher mortality, slower spread.
Egg drop syndromeEgg shell changes without respiratory signs; albumen quality normal.
MG, coryzaSlower spread, sinusitis, airsacculitis.
IBD, gout, dehydration, mycotoxins (kidneys)Other causes of swollen kidneys with urates.

Laboratory confirmation

SampleTestNotes
Tracheal swabs, lung, kidney, caecal tonsils (chilled or FTA)RT-PCR and S1 sequencingGenotyping guides vaccine choice.
SameVirus isolation in SPF eggsEmbryo dwarfing and curling after 2–3 passages.
Paired seraELISA, HIRising titre supports infection; interpret with vaccination.

Treatment, control and prevention

  • No specific treatment; keep birds warm, improve ventilation, electrolytes; treat secondary E. coli after culture. For nephropathogenic IB reduce dietary protein and calcium and give electrolytes.
  • Vaccinate with live vaccines (Massachusetts plus a variant strain as needed, e.g. 793B) in chicks and inactivated vaccine in layers/breeders; use strains matching local genotypes.
  • Biosecurity and all-in/all-out management.

Photographs

lessons.title: Infectious laryngotracheitis (ILT)
lessons.html:
Cause: Gallid alphaherpesvirus 1 (ILT virus). Latent carriers after recovery; vaccine strains (CEO, TCO) can revert.

At a glance

Key post-mortem picture: Severe respiratory distress with gasping (neck extended), coughing up blood; haemorrhagic tracheitis with blood clots and bloody mucus; diphtheritic plaques in the larynx.

Pathognomonic / highly suggestive: Haemorrhagic tracheitis with blood clots is highly suggestive; intranuclear inclusion bodies (Cowdry type A) in syncytial tracheal epithelial cells on histology are diagnostic.

Confirm with: Histopathology of trachea/larynx (inclusion bodies, syncytia); PCR on tracheal swabs or tissue (with differentiation of vaccine strains).

Cause and epidemiology

  • Chickens over 4 weeks old, mostly layers and breeders. Spreads more slowly than IB (days to weeks through a house).
  • Morbidity 50–100 %; mortality 10–20 % (up to 70 % in severe forms). Mild forms give conjunctivitis and mild tracheitis only.

Clinical (physical) signs

  • Gasping with the neck extended on each breath, loud gurgling rales, coughing and head shaking; blood-stained mucus on the beak, face, walls and cages.
  • Conjunctivitis, swollen infraorbital sinuses (mild form).
  • Drop in egg production.

Post-mortem lesions, step by step

Examine in this order; record positive and negative findings for every bird.

Organ / siteWhat you see
Larynx and tracheaMucoid to haemorrhagic tracheitis; blood clots and bloody mucus in the lumen; yellow caseous or diphtheritic plugs in the larynx and upper trachea that can block the airway.
Conjunctiva and sinusesCongestion and oedema, sometimes caseous exudate.
Lungs and air sacsUsually normal or mildly congested.

Pathognomonic and highly suggestive lesions

  • Syncytia with intranuclear inclusion bodies in tracheal epithelium (histology).
  • Blood clots in the trachea (grossly, highly suggestive).

Differential diagnosis

DiseaseHow to tell it apart
Wet (diphtheritic) fowl poxYellow plaques in mouth and larynx; Bollinger bodies (intracytoplasmic) on histology; skin pox lesions often present.
Infectious bronchitisFaster spread, no blood in trachea.
Newcastle disease, HPAISystemic haemorrhages, nervous signs, very high mortality.
Aspergillosis, vitamin A deficiencyFungal plaques; pustules in oesophagus.

Laboratory confirmation

SampleTestNotes
Trachea and larynx in formalinHistopathologyInclusions are best seen in the first 1–5 days of illness.
Tracheal swabs or tissue (chilled)PCR; PCR-RFLP or sequencing to separate vaccine and field strains; virus isolation (CAM pocks)
SerumELISA, virus neutralisationRetrospective only.

Treatment, control and prevention

  • No treatment; reduce dust, treat secondary bacteria.
  • Vaccinate in endemic areas with live attenuated (eye drop) or recombinant vector vaccines (HVT-ILT, FP-ILT). Vaccinate the whole farm at once to avoid vaccine-strain spread.
  • Recovered birds are latent carriers: do not mix with new stock.

Photographs

lessons.title: Fowl pox
lessons.html:
Cause: Fowlpox virus (Avipoxvirus, Poxviridae). Transmitted by mosquitoes and by contact with scabs through skin wounds.

At a glance

Key post-mortem picture: Dry (cutaneous) form: wart-like nodules and scabs on comb, wattles, eyelids, beak corners and legs. Wet (diphtheritic) form: yellow cheesy plaques in the mouth, pharynx, larynx and trachea.

Pathognomonic / highly suggestive: Large eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions (Bollinger bodies) in epithelial cells are pathognomonic. Grossly, typical dry pox scabs are very characteristic.

Confirm with: Histopathology (Bollinger bodies); PCR; virus isolation on chorioallantoic membrane (CAM pocks).

Cause and epidemiology

  • All ages; common in the rainy season when mosquitoes are numerous. Spreads slowly through the flock.
  • Dry form: low mortality, slower growth and drop in lay. Wet form: higher mortality (up to 50 %) from suffocation and inability to eat.

Clinical (physical) signs

  • Grey-white small papules that grow into yellow, then dark brown wart-like scabs on featherless skin; conjunctivitis when eyelids are affected.
  • Wet form: difficult breathing, gasping, nasal and ocular discharge, reluctance to eat.

Post-mortem lesions, step by step

Examine in this order; record positive and negative findings for every bird.

Organ / siteWhat you see
SkinProliferative nodules and scabs; underneath, a moist, bleeding surface.
Mouth, pharynx, larynx, tracheaYellow, raised, diphtheritic plaques firmly attached to the mucosa; removal leaves bleeding ulcers.

Pathognomonic and highly suggestive lesions

  • Bollinger bodies (histology).

Differential diagnosis

DiseaseHow to tell it apart
ILTTracheal lesions only, blood clots; intranuclear inclusions.
Biotin or pantothenic acid deficiencyCrusts at beak corners and on feet, symmetrical; responds to diet.
Favus (Microsporum gallinae)White powdery scales on comb, not nodules.
Trichomoniasis, candidiasisMouth/crop lesions; organisms in wet smears.
Wounds, pecking, mycotoxin (T-2) mouth lesionsHistory and distribution.

Laboratory confirmation

SampleTestNotes
Scabs or plaques in formalinHistopathologyBollinger bodies confirm.
Scabs (dry or chilled)PCR; CAM inoculation

Treatment, control and prevention

  • No specific treatment; clean wet-form lesions gently, give soft feed, vitamins (especially vitamin A) and antibiotics for secondary infection.
  • Vaccinate by wing-web stab (check "take" at 7–10 days: swelling/scab at the site). Vaccinate the whole flock in the face of an outbreak.
  • Mosquito control, screens, and removal of stagnant water.

Photographs

lessons.title: Avian metapneumovirus infection and swollen head syndrome (SHS)
lessons.html:
Cause: Avian metapneumovirus (aMPV, subtypes A and B) as the primary agent, with secondary E. coli (and sometimes Ornithobacterium rhinotracheale) producing swollen head syndrome.

At a glance

Key post-mortem picture: Swelling of the periorbital and infraorbital area and of the whole head; yellow caseous or gelatinous exudate under the skin of the head; nervous signs (torticollis) in some birds; egg drop in layers.

Pathognomonic / highly suggestive: None; subcutaneous caseous exudate in the head is characteristic of SHS but E. coli is the cause of that lesion.

Confirm with: RT-PCR (aMPV) on nasal/choanal swabs early in disease; ELISA serology (paired sera); culture of E. coli from head exudate.

Cause and epidemiology

  • Broilers from 4 weeks and broiler breeders/layers; worse with poor ventilation and ammonia.
  • Morbidity may be high; mortality usually 1–5 % (higher with E. coli).

Clinical (physical) signs

  • Sneezing, foamy eyes, conjunctivitis, then swelling of the face starting around the eyes and spreading over the head and wattles.
  • Depression, head shaking, scratching; torticollis and incoordination in some birds.
  • Layers: drop in egg production (up to 30 %) and shell quality problems.

Post-mortem lesions, step by step

Examine in this order; record positive and negative findings for every bird.

Organ / siteWhat you see
Head subcutisGelatinous yellow oedema early, then yellow caseous exudate under the skin of the head, periorbital region and wattles.
Nasal cavity and sinusesCatarrhal rhinitis and sinusitis.
Middle ear, skullCaseous exudate in the middle ear and skull bones in birds with nervous signs.
OviductEgg peritonitis, misshapen eggs in layers.

Pathognomonic and highly suggestive lesions

  • None.

Differential diagnosis

DiseaseHow to tell it apart
Infectious coryzaFoul-smelling nasal discharge, facial swelling in sinuses; A. paragallinarum culture/PCR.
Chronic fowl choleraSwollen, caseous wattles; P. multocida culture.
MG sinusitisSlow onset, airsacculitis; MG serology/PCR.
HPAIHead oedema with high mortality and systemic haemorrhages.
Vitamin A deficiencyPustules in the oesophagus, caseous sinus exudate.

Laboratory confirmation

SampleTestNotes
Choanal/nasal swabs in first daysRT-PCR aMPVVirus is present only briefly.
Paired seraELISA
Head exudateBacterial culture and sensitivityFor E. coli.

Treatment, control and prevention

  • Treat secondary E. coli after culture; improve ventilation and litter, reduce ammonia.
  • Live and inactivated aMPV vaccines exist for chickens (especially breeders and layers).

Photographs

lessons.title: Fowl adenovirus infections: inclusion body hepatitis (IBH) and hydropericardium syndrome (HPS)
lessons.html:
Cause: Fowl aviadenovirus (FAdV); IBH mainly species D and E (serotypes 2, 11, 8a, 8b); HPS ("Angara disease") by FAdV-4 (species C). Vertical and horizontal transmission.

At a glance

Key post-mortem picture: Broilers 3–6 weeks: sudden rise in mortality; pericardial sac filled with clear, straw-coloured fluid (HPS); enlarged, pale, yellow, friable liver with petechiae (IBH); swollen kidneys.

Pathognomonic / highly suggestive: Large basophilic intranuclear inclusion bodies in hepatocytes are characteristic (histology). Grossly, severe hydropericardium with hepatitis in young broilers is highly suggestive of HPS.

Confirm with: Histopathology of liver; PCR (hexon gene) with sequencing to type; virus isolation in chicken liver cells.

Cause and epidemiology

  • Broilers 3–6 weeks (IBH also in young broiler breeders). Often follows immunosuppression (IBD, CAV).
  • Mortality: IBH 2–10 % (up to 30 %); HPS 20–75 %. Peak within 3–4 days, finishing in 10–14 days.

Clinical (physical) signs

  • Sudden deaths of well-grown birds; depression, ruffled feathers, huddling; birds found on their backs.
  • Pale comb, yellow droppings; anaemia in some.

Post-mortem lesions, step by step

Examine in this order; record positive and negative findings for every bird.

Organ / siteWhat you see
Pericardium (HPS)Up to 10–20 ml of clear, straw-coloured or jelly-like fluid; heart soft and flabby.
LiverEnlarged, pale, yellow-brown, friable, with petechiae and ecchymoses or necrotic foci (IBH).
KidneysEnlarged, pale, with tubular urates.
OtherLung oedema, ascites; bursa and thymus may be atrophied; enteritis; gizzard erosions (FAdV-1 gizzard erosion).

Pathognomonic and highly suggestive lesions

  • Basophilic intranuclear inclusion bodies in hepatocytes (histology).

Differential diagnosis

DiseaseHow to tell it apart
Ascites syndromeRight ventricular hypertrophy and dilatation; abdominal fluid; no hepatitis; associated with altitude, cold, fast growth.
AflatoxicosisPale fatty liver, feed history, no inclusions.
CAV, IBDImmunosuppressive predisposing infections; check bone marrow and bursa.
Salt or ionophore toxicityFeed history, hydropericardium/heart lesions without liver inclusions.
Fowl cholera, salmonellosisBacterial culture.

Laboratory confirmation

SampleTestNotes
Liver in formalinHistopathologyLook for intranuclear inclusions.
Liver, kidney (chilled)PCR (hexon), sequencing; virus isolationSerotype identification helps choose vaccine.

Treatment, control and prevention

  • No specific treatment; support with vitamins and electrolytes; reduce stress; control IBD and CAV.
  • Vaccination of breeders (and in some countries broilers) with inactivated FAdV-4 or autogenous vaccines; buy chicks from vaccinated, adenovirus-controlled breeders.

Photographs

lessons.title: Avian encephalomyelitis (AE, epidemic tremor)
lessons.html:
Cause: Avian encephalomyelitis virus (Tremovirus A, Picornaviridae). Vertical (through the egg) and horizontal (faecal-oral) transmission.

At a glance

Key post-mortem picture: Chicks 1–3 weeks: ataxia, sitting on hocks, fine tremors of head and neck; few or no gross lesions. Adults: temporary egg drop only.

Pathognomonic / highly suggestive: No gross lesions of diagnostic value. Histology: non-purulent encephalomyelitis with perivascular cuffing, central chromatolysis of neurons in the brainstem and lymphoid follicles in the muscular wall of the proventriculus and gizzard (characteristic).

Confirm with: Histopathology of brain and proventriculus; RT-PCR on brain; ELISA serology of the breeder flock.

Cause and epidemiology

  • Chicks from breeder flocks that were not immune when they came into lay; tremors from the first days to 3 weeks of age.
  • Morbidity 40–60 % of chicks, mortality up to 25 % or more (starvation, trampling).

Clinical (physical) signs

  • Dull expression, progressive incoordination, sitting on hocks, falling over; fine tremor of head and neck (seen better when the chick is held or disturbed).
  • Survivors may later develop cataracts (bluish-grey lens).
  • Layers: 5–10 % egg drop for about 2 weeks, no nervous signs.

Post-mortem lesions, step by step

Examine in this order; record positive and negative findings for every bird.

Organ / siteWhat you see
Brain and spinal cordNo gross lesions in most birds.
GizzardSmall whitish areas in the muscle (lymphoid foci), rarely visible.
OtherField cases may show non-specific changes such as swollen kidneys or mild enteritis; these are not diagnostic.

Pathognomonic and highly suggestive lesions

  • Histological lesions only (see "At a glance").

Differential diagnosis

DiseaseHow to tell it apart
Vitamin E deficiency (encephalomalacia)Older chicks (2–4 weeks); swollen, haemorrhagic, soft cerebellum.
Riboflavin deficiencyCurled toes, swollen nerves.
Newcastle diseaseRespiratory and digestive signs, older birds, PCR/HI.
Marek's diseaseOlder birds, nerve enlargement.
Brooder pneumonia (aspergillosis) with brain involvement, toxicitiesLesions in lungs/brain; history.

Laboratory confirmation

SampleTestNotes
Brain, proventriculus, pancreas in formalinHistopathology
Brain (chilled)RT-PCR, virus isolation (embryo susceptibility test)
Breeder seraELISAShows whether breeders were immune.

Treatment, control and prevention

  • No treatment; cull affected chicks.
  • Vaccinate breeders and layers with live AE vaccine (drinking water or wing web, often combined with fowl pox) at 10–16 weeks, at least 4 weeks before lay.

Photographs

lessons.title: Egg drop syndrome (EDS)
lessons.html:
Cause: Duck atadenovirus A (EDS-76 virus), spread from ducks and geese, through the egg and by contaminated trays and needles.

At a glance

Key post-mortem picture: Healthy-looking layers produce thin-shelled, soft-shelled and shell-less eggs and loss of shell pigment; production fails to reach peak or drops 10–40 %.

Pathognomonic / highly suggestive: None grossly. Histology: intranuclear inclusion bodies in the shell gland epithelium.

Confirm with: HI serology (EDS antigen); PCR on oviduct/shell gland; virus isolation in duck eggs.

Cause and epidemiology

  • Laying hens around peak production; brown-egg layers show the loss of shell colour best. Ducks and geese are carriers.

Clinical (physical) signs

  • No illness; egg problems only: pale, thin, rough, soft or shell-less eggs; more floor and broken eggs.

Post-mortem lesions, step by step

Examine in this order; record positive and negative findings for every bird.

Organ / siteWhat you see
Oviduct (shell gland)Mild oedema, exudate; often no visible lesion. Ovary: inactive or ruptured follicles in some hens.

Pathognomonic and highly suggestive lesions

  • None.

Differential diagnosis

DiseaseHow to tell it apart
Infectious bronchitisRespiratory signs, watery albumen, misshapen eggs.
Newcastle disease, LPAIIllness, mortality.
Nutritional (calcium, phosphorus, vitamin D)Feed analysis; bone quality.
Heat stress, old hens, MS (eggshell apex abnormality)History, serology.

Laboratory confirmation

SampleTestNotes
Sera (before and after the drop)HI test (EDS antigen)Rising titre.
Shell gland (chilled; formalin)PCR; histopathology

Treatment, control and prevention

  • No treatment; production recovers slowly.
  • Inactivated EDS vaccine (alone or combined with ND/IB) at 14–18 weeks of age.
  • Keep ducks and geese away; clean egg trays; avoid shared needles.

Photographs

lessons.title: Viral arthritis / tenosynovitis (reovirus)
lessons.html:
Cause: Avian orthoreovirus. Horizontal and vertical transmission.

At a glance

Key post-mortem picture: Lameness in broilers and broiler breeders (4–16 weeks); swollen hock and the tendons above it (gastrocnemius); rupture of the gastrocnemius tendon with haemorrhage.

Pathognomonic / highly suggestive: Bilateral swelling of the gastrocnemius tendon sheaths with rupture in older birds is highly characteristic.

Confirm with: RT-PCR on tendon/synovium; histopathology; serology (ELISA); virus isolation.

Cause and epidemiology

  • Mainly meat-type chickens; morbidity up to 10 %, low mortality; culls and downgrades cause losses.

Clinical (physical) signs

  • Lameness, reluctance to move, sitting; swollen hocks; in ruptured tendons the bird stands on its hocks.

Post-mortem lesions, step by step

Examine in this order; record positive and negative findings for every bird.

Organ / siteWhat you see
Hock and shankOedema and swelling of the tendon sheaths above the hock; small amount of clear or blood-tinged fluid; later fibrosis and thickening; ruptured gastrocnemius tendon with haemorrhage (green-blue discolouration).

Pathognomonic and highly suggestive lesions

  • Swollen gastrocnemius tendon sheaths / tendon rupture in meat breeds (highly characteristic).

Differential diagnosis

DiseaseHow to tell it apart
Mycoplasma synoviaeSynovitis with creamy exudate in joints and keel bursa; MS serology/PCR.
Staphylococcus aureus, E. coli arthritisPus/caseous material; culture.
Articular goutChalky urate deposits in joints.
Tibial dyschondroplasia, ricketsBone lesions.

Laboratory confirmation

SampleTestNotes
Tendon, synovium (chilled; formalin)RT-PCR; histopathology
SeraELISA

Treatment, control and prevention

  • No treatment; cull lame birds.
  • Vaccinate breeders (live then inactivated) to give maternal immunity; hygiene in hatchery and houses.

Photographs

lessons.title: Colibacillosis (Escherichia coli infections)
lessons.html:
Cause: Avian pathogenic Escherichia coli (APEC), e.g. serogroups O1, O2, O78. Mostly secondary to viral infections, MG, poor ventilation, ammonia and dust.

At a glance

Key post-mortem picture: Fibrinous polyserositis: fibrin over the heart (pericarditis), liver (perihepatitis) and air sacs (airsacculitis); also omphalitis/yolk sac infection in chicks, salpingitis and egg peritonitis in layers, cellulitis, swollen head syndrome, coligranuloma.

Pathognomonic / highly suggestive: Not pathognomonic: the triad of fibrinous pericarditis + perihepatitis + airsacculitis is typical but also caused by MG, Chlamydia and other bacteria. Diagnosis needs culture of a pure growth of E. coli from lesions.

Confirm with: Bacterial culture from heart blood, liver, air-sac exudate or bone marrow (MacConkey, blood agar); antibiotic sensitivity testing; PCR for APEC virulence genes where available.

Cause and epidemiology

  • All ages; the most common bacterial disease of poultry. Chicks are infected through the navel and contaminated eggs; older birds by inhalation of contaminated dust after the respiratory lining is damaged.
  • Predisposing factors: IB, ND, LPAI, MG, aMPV, IBD, high ammonia, dust, overcrowding, poor water quality.

Clinical (physical) signs

  • Chicks: omphalitis (wet, swollen, inflamed navel), distended abdomen, early chick mortality (first week).
  • Growing birds: respiratory signs, depression, ruffled feathers, poor growth, deaths.
  • Layers: drop in production, penguin posture from egg peritonitis, sudden deaths.
  • Cellulitis: yellow plaques under the skin of the abdomen/thigh at slaughter.

Post-mortem lesions, step by step

Examine in this order; record positive and negative findings for every bird.

Organ / siteWhat you see
Navel and yolk sac (chicks)Unabsorbed, foul-smelling, brown-green or caseous yolk; inflamed navel.
Air sacsThickened, cloudy, with yellow caseous exudate.
HeartFibrinous pericarditis: white-yellow fibrin sheet covering the heart, pericardium stuck to the epicardium.
LiverFibrinous perihepatitis (a removable film over the liver capsule); liver may be enlarged, dark, with necrotic foci.
Oviduct and abdomen (layers)Salpingitis: oviduct distended with layered caseous material; egg peritonitis: yolk and fibrin through the abdomen.
OtherSwollen spleen; arthritis; coligranulomas (nodular granulomas in liver, caeca, mesentery); cellulitis.

Pathognomonic and highly suggestive lesions

  • None. Pure culture from typical lesions confirms.

Differential diagnosis

DiseaseHow to tell it apart
Mycoplasma gallisepticum (CRD)Often together with E. coli; MG serology/PCR.
ChlamydiosisFibrinous serositis with enlarged spleen; PCR; zoonotic.
Fowl cholera, salmonellosisPasteurella or Salmonella isolated.
Visceral goutChalky urate (not fibrin) on serosae; dissolves differently, kidneys damaged.
Avian TBColigranuloma resembles TB tubercles; acid-fast stain.

Laboratory confirmation

SampleTestNotes
Heart blood, liver, spleen, air sac, bone marrow, yolk sacCulture on MacConkey/blood agar; biochemical ID; sensitivity testSample freshly dead or euthanised birds before treatment.
IsolatePCR for virulence genes, serotypingHelps separate APEC from gut E. coli.

Treatment, control and prevention

  • Treat with an antibiotic chosen by sensitivity testing (resistance is widespread); respect egg and meat withdrawal times.
  • Remove the primary cause: control MG, IB, ND; improve ventilation; reduce ammonia and dust; chlorinate water.
  • Hatchery hygiene: clean eggs, fumigation, discard floor/cracked eggs. Autogenous or live E. coli vaccines are used in some systems.

Photographs

lessons.title: Fowl cholera (pasteurellosis)
lessons.html:
Cause: Pasteurella multocida (Gram-negative, bipolar-staining coccobacillus). Carriers, wild birds, rodents and cats spread it.

At a glance

Key post-mortem picture: Acute: sudden deaths in adult birds; petechiae on heart and coronary fat; many pinpoint white necrotic foci in the liver; "cooked" or flaccid ovarian follicles and yolk peritonitis. Chronic: swollen wattles filled with caseous material, swollen joints and sinuses.

Pathognomonic / highly suggestive: None strictly; bipolar-staining organisms in liver or heart-blood impression smears with the lesions above are highly suggestive.

Confirm with: Culture of P. multocida from liver, heart blood, bone marrow (blood agar, no growth on MacConkey); PCR (kmt1); impression smear (Wright, Giemsa or methylene blue: bipolar rods).

Cause and epidemiology

  • Birds over 16 weeks, mostly layers and breeders in lay; turkeys and ducks are more susceptible.
  • Acute outbreaks may kill 20 % or more of a flock; chronic infection persists in carriers.

Clinical (physical) signs

  • Acute: sudden death, fever, depression, cyanosis, mucous discharge from mouth, greenish-yellow or watery diarrhoea, rapid breathing, drop in egg production.
  • Chronic: swollen wattles (localised infection), swollen face and sinuses, conjunctivitis, lameness from swollen joints, torticollis (middle ear infection).

Post-mortem lesions, step by step

Examine in this order; record positive and negative findings for every bird.

Organ / siteWhat you see
Heart and fatPetechiae and ecchymoses on the epicardium, coronary fat and abdominal fat; pericardial fluid increased.
LiverEnlarged, with many pinpoint grey-white foci of necrosis.
Ovary and abdomenCongested, flaccid, "cooked-looking" or ruptured follicles; yolk in the abdomen; fibrinous peritonitis.
Lungs and gutPneumonia (especially in turkeys); duodenal enteritis.
ChronicWattles filled with yellow caseous exudate; fibrinopurulent arthritis; caseous sinusitis and otitis.

Pathognomonic and highly suggestive lesions

  • None. Heart petechiae + liver necrotic foci + ovarian lesions in an adult bird with bipolar bacteria in smears = strongly supportive.

Differential diagnosis

DiseaseHow to tell it apart
HPAI, velogenic NDVery similar acute picture; exclude by PCR before treating as fowl cholera.
Fowl typhoidBronze liver, splenomegaly, anaemia; Salmonella Gallinarum culture.
ColibacillosisFibrinous polyserositis; E. coli culture.
ErysipelasTurkeys mostly; Gram-positive rods.
Infectious coryza (chronic form)Swollen face without caseous wattles; A. paragallinarum.

Laboratory confirmation

SampleTestNotes
Liver, heart blood, bone marrow, wattle exudateImpression smear (bipolar rods); culture on blood agar; PCR; sensitivityBone marrow (from the femur) is the best sample in decomposed birds.
SerumAgglutination testsLimited use.

Treatment, control and prevention

  • Treat early with an antibiotic according to sensitivity (e.g. sulfonamides, tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones where legally permitted), respecting egg withdrawal; outbreaks often recur after treatment stops.
  • Remove chronic carriers; control rodents, cats and wild birds; all-in/all-out.
  • Vaccinate in endemic farms with inactivated bacterins (two doses before lay) or live vaccines.

Photographs

lessons.title: Fowl typhoid and pullorum disease (Salmonella Gallinarum / Pullorum)
lessons.html:
Cause: Salmonella enterica serovar Gallinarum, biovars Gallinarum (fowl typhoid) and Pullorum (pullorum disease). Host-adapted to poultry; vertical (egg) and horizontal transmission.

At a glance

Key post-mortem picture: Fowl typhoid (growers/adults): enlarged, friable, bronze-green liver (after exposure to air), enlarged spleen, anaemia, pale comb. Pullorum (chicks under 3 weeks): white diarrhoea pasting the vent, grey-white nodules in lungs, heart, gizzard; caecal cores; unabsorbed yolk.

Pathognomonic / highly suggestive: Bronze-green discolouration of the liver is highly characteristic of fowl typhoid; in adult carriers of pullorum, misshapen, discoloured, pedunculated ovarian follicles are highly suggestive.

Confirm with: Culture (liver, spleen, caecal tonsils, ovary; pre-enrichment and selective media such as selenite broth, XLD, brilliant green agar) with serotyping; rapid whole-blood or serum plate agglutination test for flock screening.

Cause and epidemiology

  • Fowl typhoid: important in brown-egg layers in Africa, Asia and Latin America; mortality can reach 60–80 %. Pullorum: chicks in the first 2–3 weeks, from infected breeder flocks and hatcheries.

Clinical (physical) signs

  • Fowl typhoid: sudden deaths, depression, pale and shrunken comb and wattles (anaemia), ruffled feathers, green-yellow diarrhoea, drop in egg production.
  • Pullorum: chicks huddled near heat, white chalky diarrhoea pasting the vent ("pasty butt"), gasping, lameness from swollen joints, high mortality in the first 2 weeks.
  • Adult pullorum carriers often show no signs.

Post-mortem lesions, step by step

Examine in this order; record positive and negative findings for every bird.

Organ / siteWhat you see
Liver (typhoid)Swollen, friable, bronze or greenish-brown colour that deepens after exposure to air; small necrotic foci.
Spleen (typhoid)Enlarged, sometimes with necrotic foci.
Blood (typhoid)Thin, watery (anaemia); pale carcass.
Heart (both)Grey-white nodules in the myocardium; pericarditis.
Chicks (pullorum)Unabsorbed yolk; grey nodules in lungs, liver, heart and gizzard wall; white caseous cores in caeca; enteritis; swollen joints.
Adult carriers (pullorum)Misshapen, cystic, discoloured, pedunculated (stalked) ovarian follicles; peritonitis; pericarditis.

Pathognomonic and highly suggestive lesions

  • Bronze-green liver (typhoid); pedunculated abnormal follicles in adults (pullorum), both highly suggestive.

Differential diagnosis

DiseaseHow to tell it apart
Fowl choleraPasteurella in smears/culture; heart petechiae.
Colibacillosis, omphalitisFibrinous polyserositis; E. coli culture.
Aspergillosis (chicks)Lung nodules contain fungal hyphae.
Marek's diseaseHeart nodules are lymphoid tumours.
Paratyphoid salmonellae, campylobacter hepatitisCulture and serotyping.

Laboratory confirmation

SampleTestNotes
Liver, spleen, caecal tonsils, ovary, yolkCulture with enrichment; serotyping; sensitivity; PCR
Whole blood or serum of breeders/layersRapid plate agglutination with stained pullorum antigen; ELISAPositive reactors confirmed by culture.

Treatment, control and prevention

  • Antibiotics reduce mortality but do not eliminate carriers; treated flocks remain infected.
  • Test-and-slaughter of breeders; buy chicks only from pullorum/typhoid-free sources; hatchery hygiene; rodent control; all-in/all-out.
  • Live (9R) or inactivated fowl typhoid vaccines in endemic areas (layers).

Photographs

lessons.title: Mycoplasmosis: M. gallisepticum (CRD) and M. synoviae
lessons.html:
Cause: Mycoplasma gallisepticum (MG) and Mycoplasma synoviae (MS). Vertical (through the egg) and horizontal transmission.

At a glance

Key post-mortem picture: MG: chronic respiratory disease with catarrhal rhinitis, sinusitis (swollen face in turkeys, "owl head"), tracheitis and airsacculitis with foamy then caseous exudate; complicated by E. coli ("complicated CRD"). MS: synovitis, swollen hocks and foot pads, sternal bursitis, eggshell apex abnormalities, airsacculitis.

Pathognomonic / highly suggestive: None; foamy air-sac exudate is suggestive of MG. Eggshell apex abnormalities (thin rough cap) are characteristic of MS.

Confirm with: Serology: rapid serum agglutination (screen), ELISA, HI (confirm); PCR on tracheal/choanal swabs or joint exudate; culture on Frey's medium.

Cause and epidemiology

  • All ages; slow spread; disease worse with ND/IB vaccination reactions, ammonia, dust and E. coli.
  • Losses: poor feed conversion, egg drop (10–20 %), condemnations, and in breeders reduced hatchability.

Clinical (physical) signs

  • MG: nasal discharge, coughing, tracheal rales, foamy eyes, swollen infraorbital sinuses, reduced feed intake and egg production.
  • MS: lameness, swollen hocks and foot pads, breast blisters, pale comb, green droppings; or subclinical airsacculitis.

Post-mortem lesions, step by step

Examine in this order; record positive and negative findings for every bird.

Organ / siteWhat you see
Nasal passages, sinusesCatarrhal exudate; caseous exudate in swollen sinuses.
TracheaCatarrhal tracheitis, thickened mucosa.
Air sacsThickened, cloudy, with foamy exudate early, then yellow caseous material.
Heart, liver (complicated CRD)Fibrinous pericarditis and perihepatitis (E. coli).
Joints (MS)Creamy-grey to caseous exudate in hock, foot pad and keel bursa; later orange staining and erosion of cartilage.

Pathognomonic and highly suggestive lesions

  • None.

Differential diagnosis

DiseaseHow to tell it apart
Infectious coryzaFaster onset, foul smell, A. paragallinarum.
IB, ND, LPAI, aMPVViral respiratory diseases; PCR/serology.
Colibacillosis aloneCulture; MG negative.
Viral arthritis, staphylococcal arthritis (for MS)Tendon lesions or pus; PCR/culture.

Laboratory confirmation

SampleTestNotes
Serum (20 birds)RSA (screen), ELISA, HI (confirm)RSA false positives occur after inactivated oil vaccines.
Choanal cleft/tracheal swabs, air sac, joint exudatePCR (preferred); culture

Treatment, control and prevention

  • Treat with tylosin, tiamulin, tilmicosin, doxycycline or enrofloxacin according to local rules and withdrawal times; reduces signs but does not clear infection.
  • Buy MG/MS-free stock; all-in/all-out single-age farms; live vaccines (ts-11, 6/85, F strain; MS-H) or inactivated bacterins in multi-age layer farms.

Photographs

lessons.title: Infectious coryza
lessons.html:
Cause: Avibacterium paragallinarum (formerly Haemophilus paragallinarum), serovars A, B, C. Carrier birds maintain it on multi-age farms.

At a glance

Key post-mortem picture: Acute catarrhal inflammation of the nasal passages and infraorbital sinuses: facial swelling, foul-smelling nasal discharge, conjunctivitis, swollen wattles; short incubation (1–3 days).

Pathognomonic / highly suggestive: None grossly. Satellite growth of the organism around a Staphylococcus "nurse" streak (NAD-dependence) supports identification.

Confirm with: Culture from sinus exudate (chocolate agar or blood agar with Staphylococcus nurse streak, CO2); PCR (HPG-2); serology (HI) for serovar.

Cause and epidemiology

  • Growing and adult chickens; spreads through water and direct contact; multi-age farms keep it going.
  • High morbidity, low mortality (unless complicated with MG, E. coli, fowl pox); egg drop 10–40 %.

Clinical (physical) signs

  • Swelling of face and wattles (one or both sides), sticky, foul-smelling nasal discharge, eyelids stuck together, sneezing, reduced feed and water intake, diarrhoea; drop in egg production.

Post-mortem lesions, step by step

Examine in this order; record positive and negative findings for every bird.

Organ / siteWhat you see
Nasal cavity and infraorbital sinusesCatarrhal to caseous exudate, mucosal hyperaemia.
Conjunctiva and subcutis of face/wattlesOedema and caseous exudate.
Lower respiratory tractUsually normal unless complicated (tracheitis, airsacculitis).

Pathognomonic and highly suggestive lesions

  • None.

Differential diagnosis

DiseaseHow to tell it apart
MGSlower onset; airsacculitis; MG serology/PCR.
Chronic fowl choleraCaseous wattles; P. multocida.
aMPV/SHSSubcutaneous caseous head exudate; aMPV PCR.
Vitamin A deficiencyWhite pustules in oesophagus, urates in kidneys.
ILT (mild form), ND, AITracheal and systemic lesions; PCR.

Laboratory confirmation

SampleTestNotes
Deep swab of the infraorbital sinus (cut through the skin of the sinus with sterile scissors)Culture with nurse streak; PCRSample 2–3 acutely ill, untreated birds.

Treatment, control and prevention

  • Treat early with sulfonamides, erythromycin, tetracyclines or other antibiotics according to sensitivity and local rules; relapses are common.
  • Depopulate carriers where possible; single-age farms; bacterins (containing the local serovars) given twice before lay.

Photographs

lessons.title: Necrotic enteritis
lessons.html:
Cause: Clostridium perfringens type G (NetB toxin) in the small intestine. Predisposed by coccidiosis, high-protein (fishmeal), wheat/barley diets, sudden feed changes, removal of in-feed antimicrobials.

At a glance

Key post-mortem picture: Broilers 2–6 weeks: sudden death; jejunum and ileum distended with gas, thin and friable, foul-smelling; mucosa covered by a yellow-brown or green diphtheritic pseudomembrane ("Turkish towel" appearance).

Pathognomonic / highly suggestive: The diphtheritic "Turkish towel" mucosal lesion of the small intestine is highly characteristic.

Confirm with: Gram-stained mucosal smear (many large Gram-positive rods); anaerobic culture; PCR for netB/toxin genes; histopathology (coagulative necrosis with rods).

Cause and epidemiology

  • Broilers and young pullets; acute mortality 1–2 % a day (up to 10–50 % over the outbreak); subclinical form causes poor growth and liver condemnations (cholangiohepatitis).

Clinical (physical) signs

  • Sudden deaths, depression, ruffled feathers, reluctance to move, dark brown to black or bloody diarrhoea; wet litter; poor growth in subclinical cases.

Post-mortem lesions, step by step

Examine in this order; record positive and negative findings for every bird.

Organ / siteWhat you see
Small intestine (jejunum, ileum)Distended with gas and foul fluid; thin, friable wall; mucosa covered by a tan, yellow or green adherent pseudomembrane; in early cases small focal ulcers.
LiverSwollen, with pale foci (cholangiohepatitis) in subclinical cases.
CaecaUsually normal; check for concurrent coccidiosis.

Pathognomonic and highly suggestive lesions

  • Diphtheritic "Turkish towel" small-intestinal mucosa with gas distension (highly characteristic).

Differential diagnosis

DiseaseHow to tell it apart
Coccidiosis (E. maxima, E. necatrix, E. brunetti)Oocysts/schizonts in scrapings; often occurs together.
Ulcerative enteritis (C. colinum)Deep round ulcers in lower intestine and caeca, liver necrosis; quail more affected.
Salmonellosis, NDCulture, PCR; ND has proventricular lesions.
Mycotoxin enteritisFeed history.

Laboratory confirmation

SampleTestNotes
Fresh intestinal mucosaGram-stained smear; anaerobic culture; PCR (netB)Sample within 1 hour of death (C. perfringens overgrows after death).
Intestine in formalinHistopathology
ScrapingsCoccidia examinationAlways check for predisposing coccidiosis.

Treatment, control and prevention

  • Treat with amoxicillin, bacitracin, penicillin, tylosin or lincomycin in drinking water (per local regulation and sensitivity).
  • Control coccidiosis; avoid sudden feed changes; limit fishmeal and indigestible proteins; add enzymes to wheat/barley diets; probiotics, organic acids; keep litter dry.

Photographs

lessons.title: Avian tuberculosis
lessons.html:
Cause: Mycobacterium avium subsp. avium. Very persistent in soil; zoonotic risk for immunocompromised people.

At a glance

Key post-mortem picture: Old birds (backyard flocks, long-lived breeders): progressive emaciation; grey-white to yellow, firm, caseous tubercles in liver, spleen, intestine and bone marrow.

Pathognomonic / highly suggestive: Acid-fast bacilli in caseous tubercles (Ziehl–Neelsen stain) with typical lesions confirm.

Confirm with: Ziehl–Neelsen stain of lesion smears; histopathology (granulomas with many acid-fast bacilli); culture (slow, 2–8 weeks); PCR; tuberculin wattle test in live birds.

Cause and epidemiology

  • Mainly older birds in backyard and village flocks; commercial short-lived flocks rarely affected.

Clinical (physical) signs

  • Progressive wasting despite good appetite, breast muscle atrophy ("sharp keel"), pale comb, diarrhoea, lameness (bone/joint lesions).

Post-mortem lesions, step by step

Examine in this order; record positive and negative findings for every bird.

Organ / siteWhat you see
Liver and spleenMany irregular grey-white to yellow nodules (pinhead to several cm), firm and caseous on the cut surface; no calcification.
IntestineTubercles in the wall, often ulcerating into the lumen.
Bone marrow, jointsTubercles in long bones and joints.
LungsRarely affected (unlike mammals).

Pathognomonic and highly suggestive lesions

  • Caseous tubercles containing acid-fast bacilli.

Differential diagnosis

DiseaseHow to tell it apart
Coligranuloma (Hjarre's disease)Similar granulomas; E. coli culture; no acid-fast bacilli.
Marek's disease, lymphoid leukosisSoft, homogeneous tumours; histology.
HistomoniasisTarget-shaped liver lesions and caecal cores.
Tapeworm nodules (Raillietina echinobothrida)Nodules in intestinal wall with worms attached.

Laboratory confirmation

SampleTestNotes
Lesion smearsZiehl–Neelsen stainMany acid-fast rods.
Lesions in formalinHistopathology
Fresh lesionsCulture, PCRHandle as zoonotic.

Treatment, control and prevention

  • Treatment is not recommended. Depopulate infected flocks, remove litter and topsoil, disinfect with phenolics; restock on clean ground.

Photographs

lessons.title: Staphylococcosis and bumblefoot
lessons.html:
Cause: Staphylococcus aureus (also other bacteria) entering through skin wounds, foot-pad damage or the navel.

At a glance

Key post-mortem picture: Swollen, hot foot pad with a dark scab and caseous core (bumblefoot); arthritis and tenosynovitis; osteomyelitis (femoral head necrosis); gangrenous dermatitis (with Clostridium).

Pathognomonic / highly suggestive: None; culture confirms.

Confirm with: Culture of joint/abscess material (blood agar, coagulase test); sensitivity.

Cause and epidemiology

  • Heavy birds, breeders, birds on hard, wet or rough floors or perches; injuries and immunosuppression predispose.

Clinical (physical) signs

  • Lameness, swollen joints or foot pads, sitting; fever and deaths in septicaemic forms.

Post-mortem lesions, step by step

Examine in this order; record positive and negative findings for every bird.

Organ / siteWhat you see
Foot padAbscess with yellow caseous material under a dark scab.
Joints and tendon sheathsTurbid, then caseous exudate.
BoneYellow necrotic foci at the growth plate (proximal femur, tibia).

Pathognomonic and highly suggestive lesions

  • None.

Differential diagnosis

DiseaseHow to tell it apart
MS synovitis, viral arthritisSerology/PCR, tendon lesions.
E. coli arthritisCulture.
Articular goutChalky white urate crystals.
Pododermatitis from wet litter (contact dermatitis)Superficial foot-pad burns without abscess.

Laboratory confirmation

SampleTestNotes
Abscess or joint exudateCulture, coagulase test, sensitivity

Treatment, control and prevention

  • Surgical debridement and antibiotic treatment for valuable birds; cull others.
  • Smooth perches, dry litter, trim sharp edges, control immunosuppression, hatchery hygiene.

Photographs

lessons.title: Aspergillosis (brooder pneumonia)
lessons.html:
Cause: Aspergillus fumigatus (also A. flavus and others). Spores from mouldy litter, feed and dirty hatcheries.

At a glance

Key post-mortem picture: Chicks: gasping, high mortality in the first weeks; yellow-white, firm nodules (1–5 mm) in lungs and air sacs. Older birds: thickened air sacs with yellow plaques covered by a green-grey velvety mould.

Pathognomonic / highly suggestive: Visible sporulating fungal colonies (green-grey velvet) on air-sac plaques are practically pathognomonic; septate, 45°-branching hyphae in a wet mount confirm.

Confirm with: Wet mount of lesion in 10–20 % KOH or lactophenol cotton blue (septate hyphae, conidiophores); culture on Sabouraud dextrose agar; histopathology (granulomas with hyphae; PAS/GMS stains).

Cause and epidemiology

  • Chicks (hatchery-acquired) and birds of any age in dusty, mouldy conditions; non-contagious between birds.

Clinical (physical) signs

  • Gasping, rapid breathing without rales, sleepiness, loss of appetite; nervous signs (brain infection) or eye infection (cloudy eye with a yellow plaque) in some.

Post-mortem lesions, step by step

Examine in this order; record positive and negative findings for every bird.

Organ / siteWhat you see
LungsMultiple white-yellow firm nodules, cheese-like on the cut surface.
Air sacsThickened, with yellow plaques; in older lesions a green-grey fuzzy mould growth.
Trachea, syrinxFungal plaques at the syrinx cause gasping.
OtherBrain, eye, liver lesions in disseminated cases.

Pathognomonic and highly suggestive lesions

  • Sporulating mould on air-sac lesions; hyphae in wet mounts.

Differential diagnosis

DiseaseHow to tell it apart
Pullorum diseaseLung nodules without hyphae; Salmonella culture.
Colibacillosis, MGAirsacculitis without fungal elements.
ILT, IBViral respiratory disease; PCR.
TuberculosisAcid-fast bacilli; old birds.

Laboratory confirmation

SampleTestNotes
Lesion materialKOH/lactophenol wet mountQuick, cheap, done on the farm with a microscope.
LesionsCulture on Sabouraud agar; histopathology
Litter, feed, hatchery airFungal culture (settle plates)Find the source.

Treatment, control and prevention

  • Treatment is not practical in flocks; remove the source: replace mouldy litter and feed, improve ventilation, clean and fumigate the hatchery. Copper sulphate or antifungals in water are used as adjuncts.

Photographs

lessons.title: Favus (dermatophytosis)
lessons.html:
Cause: Microsporum gallinae (Trichophyton gallinae).

At a glance

Key post-mortem picture: White, powdery, chalky scales on the comb and wattles, which may spread to feathered skin with feather loss.

Pathognomonic / highly suggestive: None; fungal elements in skin scrapings confirm.

Confirm with: Skin scraping in KOH; fungal culture.

Cause and epidemiology

  • Sporadic, mainly in older and backyard birds; zoonotic (ringworm).

Clinical (physical) signs

  • White scurfy spots coalescing into crusts on the comb; honeycomb-like crusts; feather loss on neck.

Post-mortem lesions, step by step

Examine in this order; record positive and negative findings for every bird.

Organ / siteWhat you see
SkinSuperficial white crusts; no internal lesions.

Pathognomonic and highly suggestive lesions

  • None.

Differential diagnosis

DiseaseHow to tell it apart
Fowl poxNodular scabs; Bollinger bodies.
Biotin deficiencyCrusts at beak and feet.
MitesMites visible.

Laboratory confirmation

SampleTestNotes
ScrapingsKOH wet mount, culture

Treatment, control and prevention

  • Topical antifungals (e.g. enilconazole, miconazole) in valuable birds; isolate affected birds; wear gloves.

Photographs

lessons.title: Coccidiosis
lessons.html:
Cause: Eimeria spp. (protozoa). Seven species in chickens; the site of lesions identifies the species: E. acervulina (duodenum), E. maxima (mid-intestine), E. necatrix (mid-intestine, schizonts; oocysts in caeca), E. tenella (caeca), E. brunetti (lower intestine, rectum), E. mitis and E. praecox (mild).

At a glance

Key post-mortem picture: E. tenella: caeca distended with blood and clotted cores; bloody droppings. E. necatrix: ballooned mid-intestine with "salt and pepper" white spots and petechiae on the serosa. E. acervulina: white transverse ladder-like streaks in the duodenum. E. maxima: thickened mid-gut with orange mucus and petechiae.

Pathognomonic / highly suggestive: Lesions in their typical location, together with oocysts or schizonts in a mucosal scraping from that site, are diagnostic.

Confirm with: Wet mount of mucosal scrapings (oocysts, schizonts, gametocytes) at each lesion site; oocyst counts per gram of faeces (McMaster); lesion scoring (Johnson and Reid 0–4); PCR for species.

Cause and epidemiology

  • Birds 3–8 weeks on litter; outbreaks with wet litter, overcrowding, poor anticoccidial control or poor vaccine cycling; immunosuppression (IBD, mycotoxins) worsens disease.
  • Oocysts survive for months in litter; sporulation needs warmth and moisture (1–2 days).

Clinical (physical) signs

  • E. tenella/E. necatrix: bloody droppings, pale combs, drooping wings, huddling, high mortality.
  • E. acervulina/E. maxima: watery or mucoid diarrhoea (orange mucus with E. maxima), poor growth and feed conversion, loss of pigmentation.
  • Birds recover in 7–10 days if they survive; subclinical disease reduces performance.

Post-mortem lesions, step by step

Examine in this order; record positive and negative findings for every bird.

Organ / siteWhat you see
Duodenum (E. acervulina)White, oval or transverse ladder-like plaques visible from the serosa and mucosa; thickened wall in heavy infections.
Mid-intestine (E. maxima)Thickened, ballooned wall; orange-red mucus; petechiae.
Mid-intestine (E. necatrix)Marked ballooning; white spots (schizonts) mixed with red petechiae on the serosa ("salt and pepper"); blood and mucus in the lumen.
Caeca (E. tenella)Enlarged caeca full of blood, later firm blood-and-necrotic cores; thickened wall with petechiae.
Lower intestine and rectum (E. brunetti)Coagulative necrosis, mucoid bloody enteritis.

Pathognomonic and highly suggestive lesions

  • E. tenella caecal haemorrhage with blood cores (highly characteristic).
  • Oocysts/schizonts in scrapings from lesion sites (diagnostic).

Differential diagnosis

DiseaseHow to tell it apart
Necrotic enteritisGas, friable intestine, "Turkish towel" pseudomembrane; often concurrent.
HistomoniasisCaecal cores plus target liver lesions; no oocysts.
ND, salmonellosisOther lesions; PCR, culture.
Pullorum (caecal cores in chicks)Culture.

Laboratory confirmation

SampleTestNotes
Mucosal scrapings from duodenum, mid-gut, caeca (fresh bird)Wet mount at ×100–×400Examine within 30 minutes; record the site.
Pooled fresh faeces/litterFlotation, McMaster OPGOocyst counts do not always match severity.
IntestinesLesion scoring (0–4 per species)Score 5 birds per house to monitor programmes.

Treatment, control and prevention

  • Treat with toltrazuril, amprolium, sulfonamides (e.g. sulfaquinoxaline, sulfadimethoxine), or diclazuril in water per label; add vitamin A and K.
  • Prevention: in-feed anticoccidials (ionophores, chemicals) with shuttle/rotation programmes, or live coccidiosis vaccines (not together with anticoccidials); keep litter dry; fix leaking drinkers.

Photographs

lessons.title: Histomoniasis (blackhead)
lessons.html:
Cause: Histomonas meleagridis (protozoon), carried inside eggs of the caecal worm Heterakis gallinarum and in earthworms. Chickens are often carriers; turkeys suffer severe disease.

At a glance

Key post-mortem picture: Caeca enlarged with thickened walls and yellow caseous cores; liver with circular, depressed, yellow-green "target" or "bull's-eye" necrotic foci.

Pathognomonic / highly suggestive: Target-shaped, depressed necrotic liver foci together with caseous caecal cores are practically pathognomonic (especially in turkeys).

Confirm with: Histopathology (histomonads in caecal and liver lesions); PCR; wet mount of caecal content (motile trophozoites).

Cause and epidemiology

  • Turkeys (high mortality) and chickens (usually mild caecal disease, occasional liver lesions); ranges shared with chickens carrying Heterakis.

Clinical (physical) signs

  • Depression, drooping wings, sulphur-yellow droppings; cyanosis of head in turkeys ("blackhead", not specific).

Post-mortem lesions, step by step

Examine in this order; record positive and negative findings for every bird.

Organ / siteWhat you see
CaecaEnlarged, thick-walled, inflamed; laminated yellow caseous cores.
LiverRound, depressed, yellow to green necrotic areas with raised edges, up to 1–2 cm.

Pathognomonic and highly suggestive lesions

  • Target liver lesions + caecal cores.

Differential diagnosis

DiseaseHow to tell it apart
Coccidiosis (E. tenella)Oocysts; no liver target lesions.
Salmonellosis, avian TB, tumoursCulture, histology.

Laboratory confirmation

SampleTestNotes
Caeca, liver in formalin; fresh caecal contentHistopathology, PCR, wet mount

Treatment, control and prevention

  • Few drugs remain legal in food animals; prevention by keeping turkeys away from chickens and controlling Heterakis with regular deworming.

Photographs

lessons.title: Internal worms: Ascaridia, Heterakis and tapeworms
lessons.html:
Cause: Ascaridia galli (large roundworm, 5–12 cm, small intestine); Heterakis gallinarum (caecal worm, 1–1.5 cm, carries Histomonas); Capillaria spp. (hair-like, crop, oesophagus, intestine); tapeworms such as Raillietina echinobothrida, R. tetragona and Davainea proglottina (intermediate hosts: ants, beetles, slugs, snails).

At a glance

Key post-mortem picture: Worms visible in the gut; heavy Ascaridia loads block the intestine; Capillaria cause thickened, inflamed crop and gut; R. echinobothrida causes nodules in the intestinal wall ("nodular tapeworm disease").

Pathognomonic / highly suggestive: Finding the parasite is diagnostic; nodules with an attached scolex of R. echinobothrida are characteristic.

Confirm with: Gross identification; mucosal scrapings (Capillaria, small tapeworms like Davainea); faecal flotation (thick-shelled oval eggs of ascarids; bipolar-plugged eggs of Capillaria).

Cause and epidemiology

  • Free-range, deep-litter and backyard flocks, especially on old ground and where insects are plentiful.

Clinical (physical) signs

  • Poor growth, weight loss, pale combs, diarrhoea, drop in egg production; worms occasionally found in eggs (Ascaridia migrating up the oviduct).

Post-mortem lesions, step by step

Examine in this order; record positive and negative findings for every bird.

Organ / siteWhat you see
Small intestineAscaridia: many large white worms, sometimes causing obstruction; catarrhal enteritis. Tapeworms: flat segmented worms attached to the mucosa; with R. echinobothrida, nodules on serosal and mucosal surfaces.
CaecaHeterakis: small white worms in caecal content.
Crop and oesophagusCapillaria: thickened, inflamed mucosa with hair-like worms (visible in scrapings).

Pathognomonic and highly suggestive lesions

  • Identification of the parasite.

Differential diagnosis

DiseaseHow to tell it apart
Avian TBTapeworm nodules resemble tubercles but contain worms, no acid-fast bacilli.
Coccidiosis, necrotic enteritisScrapings, lesions.

Laboratory confirmation

SampleTestNotes
FaecesFlotation (McMaster)
WormsIdentification (70 % alcohol)
Mucosal scrapingsMicroscopyFor Capillaria and small tapeworms.

Treatment, control and prevention

  • Deworm with benzimidazoles (flubendazole, fenbendazole) or levamisole for roundworms; praziquantel or flubendazole for tapeworms; observe egg withdrawal.
  • Control insects (intermediate hosts), rotate runs, keep litter dry, and deworm on a schedule based on faecal egg counts.

Photographs

lessons.title: External parasites: red mite, northern fowl mite, lice and fleas
lessons.html:
Cause: Dermanyssus gallinae (poultry red mite; hides in cracks by day, feeds at night), Ornithonyssus sylviarum (northern fowl mite; stays on bird), Menopon gallinae and other lice, Echidnophaga gallinacea (sticktight flea), Knemidocoptes mutans (scaly-leg mite).

At a glance

Key post-mortem picture: Anaemia (pale comb and carcass), restlessness, feather damage, drop in egg production, blood spots on eggs; mites or lice visible on birds or in the house.

Pathognomonic / highly suggestive: Finding the parasite is diagnostic.

Confirm with: Inspect birds at night (red mite) and by day (northern fowl mite, lice); collect in alcohol and identify under a hand lens or microscope.

Cause and epidemiology

  • All ages; red mite is a major problem in layer houses in warm climates; transmits pathogens such as Salmonella and E. coli.

Clinical (physical) signs

  • Pale combs, weakness, sudden deaths from anaemia in heavy red mite infestations; feather loss, scabby vent area (lice, northern fowl mite); thickened, crusty scales on shanks (scaly leg).

Post-mortem lesions, step by step

Examine in this order; record positive and negative findings for every bird.

Organ / siteWhat you see
CarcassPale muscles and organs, watery blood (anaemia); mites on skin or in feathers.

Pathognomonic and highly suggestive lesions

  • Identification of the parasite.

Differential diagnosis

DiseaseHow to tell it apart
Other causes of anaemiaCoccidiosis, fowl typhoid, CAV, leucocytozoonosis, aflatoxicosis.

Laboratory confirmation

SampleTestNotes
ParasitesIdentification
BloodPCV (packed cell volume)Below about 25 % indicates anaemia.

Treatment, control and prevention

  • Clean houses between flocks; treat cracks and perches (red mite) with approved acaricides, silica/diatomaceous earth, or fluralaner in water (where registered); treat birds for lice and northern fowl mite; rotate products to avoid resistance.

Photographs

parts.title: Part VI. Nutritional, metabolic and toxic diseases

lessons.title: Riboflavin (vitamin B2) deficiency: curled-toe paralysis
lessons.html:
Cause: Nutritional: inadequate riboflavin in the diet (poor premix, damaged vitamins, feed stored too long) or in breeder hens (poor hatchability).

At a glance

Key post-mortem picture: Chicks 1–3 weeks: toes curled inwards, walking on hocks, drooping wings; symmetrically enlarged, soft sciatic and brachial nerves.

Pathognomonic / highly suggestive: Curled-toe paralysis in young chicks with bilaterally swollen nerves that responds to riboflavin is characteristic.

Confirm with: Feed analysis (riboflavin); histopathology of nerves (demyelination, Schwann cell swelling); response to treatment.

Cause and epidemiology

  • Young chicks; embryonic deaths and "clubbed down" in chicks from deficient breeders.

Clinical (physical) signs

  • Toes curled inward and flexed, chicks walk on hocks with the help of wings; diarrhoea; poor growth; legs sprawled in advanced cases.

Post-mortem lesions, step by step

Examine in this order; record positive and negative findings for every bird.

Organ / siteWhat you see
NervesSciatic and brachial nerves enlarged (up to 4–5 times), soft, both sides.
OtherAtrophy of leg muscles; fatty liver in some.

Pathognomonic and highly suggestive lesions

  • Curled toes + symmetric soft nerve swelling in young chicks.

Differential diagnosis

DiseaseHow to tell it apart
Marek's diseaseOlder birds, usually one-sided firm nerve enlargement, tumours.
Avian encephalomyelitisTremors, no curled toes.
Leg deformities, ricketsBone lesions.

Laboratory confirmation

SampleTestNotes
FeedVitamin analysis
Nerves in formalinHistopathology

Treatment, control and prevention

  • Give riboflavin (vitamin B complex) in water or feed; mild cases recover in days, advanced cases do not. Correct the premix and feed storage.

Photographs

lessons.title: Biotin and pantothenic acid deficiency
lessons.html:
Cause: Nutritional (low biotin availability in wheat-based diets, rancid fats, mouldy feed; low pantothenic acid).

At a glance

Key post-mortem picture: Crusty, cracked, bleeding foot pads and toes; scabs at the corners of the beak and around the eyes; poor feathering; perosis.

Pathognomonic / highly suggestive: None; diagnosis by lesion pattern, feed analysis and response to supplementation.

Confirm with: Feed analysis; response to supplementation.

Cause and epidemiology

  • Young, fast-growing chicks; breeder deficiency lowers hatchability.

Clinical (physical) signs

  • Dermatitis of feet, beak corners and eyelids; poor growth; bent legs (perosis).

Post-mortem lesions, step by step

Examine in this order; record positive and negative findings for every bird.

Organ / siteWhat you see
SkinCrusts and fissures on feet and face.
Liver and kidneysFatty liver and kidney syndrome (biotin) in some broilers.

Pathognomonic and highly suggestive lesions

  • None.

Differential diagnosis

DiseaseHow to tell it apart
Fowl poxNodular scabs, Bollinger bodies.
Contact dermatitis from wet litterOnly on foot pads, hocks and breast.
T-2 mycotoxinMouth lesions; feed analysis.

Laboratory confirmation

SampleTestNotes
FeedVitamin analysis

Treatment, control and prevention

  • Supplement biotin and pantothenic acid; correct the premix; store feed properly.

Photographs

lessons.title: Vitamin E and selenium deficiency (encephalomalacia, exudative diathesis, myopathy)
lessons.html:
Cause: Nutritional: low vitamin E/selenium, or high levels of oxidised (rancid) fat in feed.

At a glance

Key post-mortem picture: Encephalomalacia ("crazy chick disease", 2–4 weeks): swollen, soft, haemorrhagic cerebellum with necrosis. Exudative diathesis: green-blue gelatinous subcutaneous oedema on breast and abdomen. Nutritional myopathy: white streaks in breast muscle.

Pathognomonic / highly suggestive: Swollen, softened cerebellum with haemorrhage in young chicks is characteristic of encephalomalacia.

Confirm with: Histopathology of brain/muscle; vitamin E and selenium analysis of feed and liver; response to treatment.

Cause and epidemiology

  • Chicks 2–6 weeks; feed with rancid fat or poorly stored premix.

Clinical (physical) signs

  • Ataxia, falling over, head retraction, "cycling" legs, prostration (encephalomalacia); swelling under the skin, weakness (exudative diathesis).

Post-mortem lesions, step by step

Examine in this order; record positive and negative findings for every bird.

Organ / siteWhat you see
CerebellumSwollen, soft, with petechiae and brown-green necrotic areas.
SubcutisGreen-blue gelatinous fluid (exudative diathesis).
MusclesPale white streaks (myopathy).

Pathognomonic and highly suggestive lesions

  • Cerebellar malacia in chicks (characteristic).

Differential diagnosis

DiseaseHow to tell it apart
AENo gross brain lesions, younger chicks, tremors.
NDOther systemic lesions.
Aspergillosis of brainFungal lesions.

Laboratory confirmation

SampleTestNotes
Brain, muscle in formalinHistopathology
Feed, liverVitamin E, selenium, peroxide value of fat

Treatment, control and prevention

  • Give vitamin E (and selenium within legal limits) in water or feed; add antioxidants; use fresh fat and premix.

Photographs

Note on photographs

No openly licensed photographs of encephalomalacia or exudative diathesis in poultry were found. Recognise encephalomalacia by a swollen, soft cerebellum with petechiae and green-brown necrotic areas, and exudative diathesis by green-blue gelatinous fluid under the skin of the breast and abdomen.

lessons.title: Rickets, tibial dyschondroplasia and cage layer fatigue
lessons.html:
Cause: Nutritional/metabolic: deficiency or imbalance of vitamin D3, calcium and phosphorus; mycotoxins; genetics (tibial dyschondroplasia); calcium depletion in high-producing caged layers.

At a glance

Key post-mortem picture: Rickets (young birds): soft, rubbery beak and bones that bend without breaking; beading of ribs; widened growth plates. Tibial dyschondroplasia: white plug of unmineralised cartilage under the proximal tibial growth plate. Cage layer fatigue: paralysis, soft thin bones, fractures, inactive ovary.

Pathognomonic / highly suggestive: Cartilage plug in the proximal tibia (tibial dyschondroplasia) is characteristic.

Confirm with: Bone examination (bend test, split tibia); bone ash; feed Ca, P and vitamin D3 analysis; histopathology.

Cause and epidemiology

  • Fast-growing broilers (rickets, TD); high-producing caged layers (fatigue).

Clinical (physical) signs

  • Lameness, reluctance to walk, squatting; bowed legs; layers found on their side, paralysed, thin-shelled eggs.

Post-mortem lesions, step by step

Examine in this order; record positive and negative findings for every bird.

Organ / siteWhat you see
BonesSoft, bend easily; ribs beaded at costochondral junctions, bent inwards; growth plates widened (rickets) or cartilage plug (TD); fractures of vertebrae and legs (layers).
ParathyroidsEnlarged (rickets).

Pathognomonic and highly suggestive lesions

  • Cartilage plug in the tibia (TD).

Differential diagnosis

DiseaseHow to tell it apart
Marek's disease, riboflavin deficiencyNerve lesions.
Infectious arthritisJoint exudate.
Femoral head necrosis (bacterial)Culture.

Laboratory confirmation

SampleTestNotes
BonesBone ash, histology
FeedCa, P, vitamin D3

Treatment, control and prevention

  • Correct the diet (vitamin D3, Ca:P balance); give vitamin AD3 in water in outbreaks; coarse limestone for layers; light and exercise.

Photographs

Note on photographs

Classic vitamin D/calcium/phosphorus rickets (rubbery beak, beaded ribs, widened growth plates) has no openly licensed photograph; use the lesion table and compare the growth plate with panel (A) of the scoring figure above: in rickets the whole growth plate is widened and soft, while in TD a discrete white cartilage plug sits below it.

lessons.title: Visceral and articular gout (urate deposition)
lessons.html:
Cause: Metabolic: kidney damage or dehydration causing accumulation of uric acid. Causes: nephropathogenic IB, water deprivation, excessive dietary calcium (layer feed to pullets), high protein, mycotoxins (ochratoxin, oosporein), sulfonamide overdose, vitamin A deficiency, excess sodium bicarbonate.

At a glance

Key post-mortem picture: Chalky white urate deposits over the pericardium, liver capsule, air sacs and serosae; swollen, pale kidneys with urate-filled tubules and ureters; in articular gout white urate deposits in joints.

Pathognomonic / highly suggestive: White crystalline urate film on visceral serosae is diagnostic of visceral gout (the task is to find the cause of the kidney failure).

Confirm with: Microscopy of deposits (needle-shaped urate crystals); murexide test; serum uric acid; feed analysis (calcium, protein, mycotoxins); IB PCR; water supply check.

Cause and epidemiology

  • Any age; outbreaks follow water failures, feed formulation errors or nephropathogenic IB.

Clinical (physical) signs

  • Depression, pale shrunken comb, white chalky diarrhoea, sudden deaths; swollen joints with articular gout.

Post-mortem lesions, step by step

Examine in this order; record positive and negative findings for every bird.

Organ / siteWhat you see
SerosaeThin white chalky film on pericardium, liver capsule, air sacs, mesentery.
Kidneys and uretersSwollen, pale, mottled; ureters distended with white urates; one kidney may be shrunken with the other enlarged (chronic).
JointsWhite pasty urate deposits in articular gout.

Pathognomonic and highly suggestive lesions

  • Visceral urate deposits.

Differential diagnosis

DiseaseHow to tell it apart
Fibrinous polyserositis (E. coli, MG)Fibrin is yellow, elastic, and peels in sheets; urates are chalky and gritty.
Dehydration aloneMild urate changes without serosal deposits.

Laboratory confirmation

SampleTestNotes
DepositsMicroscopy, murexide test
Feed, waterCalcium, protein, mycotoxins; water supply
Kidney swabsIB PCR

Treatment, control and prevention

  • Correct the cause: water supply, right feed for age (no layer feed to pullets), mycotoxin binders, IB vaccination; urine acidifiers (ammonium chloride) and electrolytes; reduce protein temporarily.

Photographs

lessons.title: Fatty liver haemorrhagic syndrome (FLHS)
lessons.html:
Cause: Metabolic: excess energy intake with little exercise in caged layers; high oestrogen activity; heat stress; mycotoxins; low choline, methionine, vitamin E or selenium.

At a glance

Key post-mortem picture: Overweight laying hens found dead; large amount of abdominal fat; enlarged, yellow, greasy, friable liver with haemorrhages and a large blood clot in the abdomen or under the liver capsule.

Pathognomonic / highly suggestive: Liver rupture with a large blood clot in an obese, fatty-livered layer is characteristic of FLHS.

Confirm with: Gross findings; histopathology (hepatocellular fat vacuolation, haemorrhage); feed energy review; exclude infectious hepatitis.

Cause and epidemiology

  • Caged layers in hot climates, especially at or after peak production; mortality up to 5 % over weeks.

Clinical (physical) signs

  • Sudden deaths of apparently healthy, heavy hens with pale combs; drop in egg production; overweight birds.

Post-mortem lesions, step by step

Examine in this order; record positive and negative findings for every bird.

Organ / siteWhat you see
LiverEnlarged, yellow, friable, greasy; subcapsular haematomas and large blood clots in the abdomen.
FatExcessive abdominal and visceral fat.
OvaryOften active.

Pathognomonic and highly suggestive lesions

  • Ruptured fatty liver with blood clot in obese layers.

Differential diagnosis

DiseaseHow to tell it apart
IBHYoung broilers, inclusions.
AflatoxicosisFeed analysis; kidney and bursa lesions.
Fowl cholera, fowl typhoidCulture.
Hepatitis E virus ("big liver and spleen", hepatitis-splenomegaly)Enlarged spleen, red fluid, PCR.

Laboratory confirmation

SampleTestNotes
Liver in formalinHistopathology
FeedEnergy, fat, mycotoxins

Treatment, control and prevention

  • Control body weight (restrict energy, especially before lay), increase fibre and protein balance, add choline, vitamin E, selenium, inositol; reduce heat stress; mycotoxin control.

Photographs

lessons.title: Ascites syndrome (pulmonary hypertension syndrome) in broilers
lessons.html:
Cause: Metabolic: fast-growing broilers whose heart and lungs cannot supply enough oxygen (cold, high altitude, poor ventilation, high ammonia/CO2, lung damage, sodium excess).

At a glance

Key post-mortem picture: Distended abdomen with clear or yellow fluid and fibrin clots; right ventricle dilated and hypertrophied; congested liver; lungs oedematous.

Pathognomonic / highly suggestive: Right ventricular hypertrophy (right ventricle : total ventricle weight ratio above about 0.28) with ascites is characteristic.

Confirm with: Gross lesions; RV:TV ratio; haematocrit (raised); review of ventilation and temperature.

Cause and epidemiology

  • Fast-growing male broilers from 3 weeks, worse in cold seasons and poorly ventilated houses.

Clinical (physical) signs

  • Distended, fluid-filled abdomen, cyanotic comb, laboured breathing, reluctance to move, sudden death.

Post-mortem lesions, step by step

Examine in this order; record positive and negative findings for every bird.

Organ / siteWhat you see
AbdomenClear or straw-coloured fluid with jelly-like fibrin clots.
HeartEnlarged, rounded; right ventricle dilated with thin or thickened wall; hydropericardium.
LiverCongested, enlarged, or shrunken and fibrotic with a thickened capsule.
LungsCongested, oedematous.

Pathognomonic and highly suggestive lesions

  • Right ventricular hypertrophy/dilatation with ascites.

Differential diagnosis

DiseaseHow to tell it apart
Hydropericardium syndrome (FAdV-4)Hepatitis, inclusions, younger birds, high mortality.
Salt toxicityFeed/water analysis.
Egg peritonitis, ovarian tumour (layers)Different age and lesions.
AflatoxicosisLiver lesions, feed analysis.

Laboratory confirmation

SampleTestNotes
HeartRV:TV weight ratio
Feed, waterSodium content

Treatment, control and prevention

  • Improve ventilation without chilling; control early growth (lighting programmes, feed restriction); avoid excess salt; control respiratory diseases.

Photographs

lessons.title: Aflatoxicosis and other mycotoxicoses
lessons.html:
Cause: Aflatoxins (Aspergillus flavus, A. parasiticus) in maize, groundnut cake and other feeds stored warm and damp; also ochratoxin (kidneys), T-2 toxin (mouth lesions), fumonisins, zearalenone.

At a glance

Key post-mortem picture: Pale yellow to orange, enlarged, friable liver with petechiae; swollen kidneys; atrophied bursa and thymus (immunosuppression); poor growth and feed conversion; vaccine failures; drop in egg production.

Pathognomonic / highly suggestive: None; confirmed by finding the toxin in the feed at a significant level together with compatible lesions.

Confirm with: Feed analysis (HPLC, ELISA or rapid strip tests) on properly collected feed samples; histopathology of liver (fat vacuoles, bile duct hyperplasia).

Cause and epidemiology

  • All ages; common in the rainy and humid seasons; groundnut cake and maize are the main risk ingredients in Nigeria.

Clinical (physical) signs

  • Poor growth, pale combs and shanks, bruising, lameness, reduced egg size and production, increased mortality from secondary infections.

Post-mortem lesions, step by step

Examine in this order; record positive and negative findings for every bird.

Organ / siteWhat you see
LiverEnlarged, pale yellow, friable, with haemorrhages (acute) or small and firm (chronic).
KidneysSwollen, pale.
Immune organsBursa and thymus atrophy.
OtherMuscle haemorrhages; mouth ulcers (T-2); gout (ochratoxin).

Pathognomonic and highly suggestive lesions

  • None.

Differential diagnosis

DiseaseHow to tell it apart
FLHSObese layers, blood clots.
IBHInclusions.
IBDBursal oedema, young birds.
Sulfonamide toxicityHistory.

Laboratory confirmation

SampleTestNotes
Feed (at least 500 g, several points)Mycotoxin analysisMould is not evenly distributed; sample well.
Liver, kidney in formalinHistopathology

Treatment, control and prevention

  • Remove contaminated feed; add mycotoxin binders; dry grain below 13 % moisture; clean feeders and bins; store feed in dry, ventilated places; test raw materials.

Photographs

parts.title: Part VII. Reproductive disorders and tumours

lessons.title: Egg peritonitis, salpingitis and reproductive tumours
lessons.html:
Cause: Egg (yolk) peritonitis and salpingitis: mostly E. coli (ascending from the cloaca), also after IB, LPAI, fowl cholera, MG, obesity, or trauma. Tumours in older hens: ovarian adenocarcinoma, leiomyoma, lymphoid tumours.

At a glance

Key post-mortem picture: Yolk material and fibrin free in the abdomen; oviduct distended with laminated caseous material ("lash eggs"); in old hens, firm white tumour nodules spread over the serosa and ascites (adenocarcinoma).

Pathognomonic / highly suggestive: Laminated caseous material in the oviduct = salpingitis. Diffuse firm white serosal nodules with ascites in old hens are highly suggestive of ovarian adenocarcinoma.

Confirm with: Culture from peritoneum/oviduct; histopathology for tumours; investigate primary viral causes (IB, LPAI serology/PCR).

Cause and epidemiology

  • Layers and breeders in lay; tumours in hens over 2 years (backyard, breeders).

Clinical (physical) signs

  • Upright, penguin-like posture; distended, fluctuating abdomen; drop in lay; sudden deaths.

Post-mortem lesions, step by step

Examine in this order; record positive and negative findings for every bird.

Organ / siteWhat you see
AbdomenYellow cooked-looking yolk and fibrin between organs; foul smell (E. coli); ascites with tumours.
OviductDistended with layered caseous masses; thin wall; sometimes a retained egg.
OvaryCongested, ruptured or misshapen follicles.
Serosa (tumour)Many firm white nodules on mesentery, pancreas and intestine (carcinomatosis).

Pathognomonic and highly suggestive lesions

  • See "At a glance".

Differential diagnosis

DiseaseHow to tell it apart
Fowl cholera, salmonellosisCulture.
LPAI, IB, NDEgg drop and peritonitis in the whole flock; PCR/serology.
